challenges.intro_fact: Spring is here — and so is a good moment to ask: what small changes can stick? Ireland produces 4x more food than it eats, but also generates over 1 million tonnes of food waste a year. The biggest changes often start in the kitchen.

questions.text: What percentage of Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions come from agriculture?
questions.fact: Agriculture accounts for about 35% of Ireland's total emissions — one of the highest shares in Europe. Most of that comes from livestock, particularly cattle.

questions.text: Which everyday action has the single biggest impact on an individual's carbon footprint?
questions.fact: Cutting out one long-haul flight saves more CO₂ than a year of recycling. Transport — especially aviation — is one of the highest-impact areas for individual action.

questions.text: Research shows that habits form fastest when they are tied to what?
questions.fact: Habit stacking — linking a new behaviour to an existing routine — is one of the most effective techniques in behaviour change research.

challenges.action_intro: Spring is a natural reset point. Small changes compounded over weeks add up — and April is a great month to start. Pick one or two things you can genuinely stick to.

actions.title: Pick one sustainable habit to add this week
actions.desc: Choose something small and specific — like bringing a bag to the shops or switching off standby devices before bed. Attach it to something you already do every day.

actions.title: Do a 10-minute home energy audit
actions.desc: Walk around your home and note anything that uses energy unnecessarily — old bulbs, devices on standby, gaps in doors or windows. Most fixes take minutes.
actions.carbon: Up to 100 kg CO₂/year if acted on

actions.title: Plan one meat-free day per week for April
actions.desc: Commit to one full day each week without meat for the month. That alone could save around 50–100 kg CO₂ over the month.

challenges.intro_fact: April Fools' Day — so let's sort the facts from the fiction. Only 16% of Irish people think they personally need to do more on climate, yet 72% of global emissions trace back to household behaviour. Some of the biggest climate myths are the most widely believed.

questions.text: True or false: recycling is the most impactful thing an individual can do for the climate.
options: True — recycling is the top action
False — diet change has far more impact
False — switching energy provider is bigger
True — plastic is the main issue
questions.fact: Recycling is important but relatively low impact compared to diet, transport and home heating. Shifting to a plant-rich diet can save 10x more CO₂ per year than optimising your recycling.

questions.text: Which of these has the LOWEST carbon footprint?
questions.fact: Oat milk has the lowest overall footprint when you combine carbon, land and water use. It produces about 80% less CO₂ than cow's milk and uses far less water than almond milk.

questions.text: Electric cars produce zero emissions. True or false?
options: False — they run on coal in Ireland
True — once the battery is made
questions.fact: Manufacturing an EV creates roughly 8 tonnes of CO₂ — mostly from the battery. But over its lifetime an EV still produces far less than a petrol car.

challenges.action_intro: Climate myths are everywhere — and even well-meaning people believe them. Understanding what actually matters is the first step to making changes that count.

actions.title: Check one climate 'fact' you believe and verify it
actions.desc: Pick something you think you know about climate and look it up on Our World in Data or the EPA Ireland site. You might be surprised.

actions.title: Share one surprising fact with someone today
actions.desc: Pick the most surprising thing you learned in this quiz and mention it to one person. Research shows peer conversations are more effective than media campaigns at shifting views.

challenges.intro_fact: Today is World Autism Awareness Day. Research consistently shows that time in nature improves wellbeing for everyone — reducing stress, improving focus and lifting mood. Yet access to green space in Ireland is very unequal depending on where you live.

questions.text: How much time in nature per week is linked to significantly better wellbeing, according to research?
questions.fact: A large UK study found that spending at least 2 hours per week in nature is linked to significantly better health and wellbeing — even spread across multiple short visits.

questions.text: What percentage of Irish people live within 15 minutes walk of a public green space?
questions.fact: Around 70% of Irish people live within a 15-minute walk of a public park or green space — but that drops in some suburban and rural areas without proper footpaths.

questions.text: Which Irish initiative aims to increase biodiversity by letting parts of public parks grow wild?
questions.fact: The All-Ireland Pollinator Plan encourages councils, farmers and households to let grass grow longer, plant wildflowers and reduce pesticide use. Over 1,000 organisations have signed up.

challenges.action_intro: Access to green space isn't just nice to have — it is a public health issue. Small actions across thousands of gardens genuinely add up for biodiversity.

actions.title: Spend 30 minutes outside in a green space this week
actions.desc: It doesn't have to be wild — a local park counts. Leave the headphones behind if you can and just notice what's around you.

actions.title: Let a patch of your garden or windowsill go wild
actions.desc: Stop cutting one corner of the lawn, or plant a small pot of wildflowers on your windowsill. Even tiny wild patches support pollinators in urban areas.

challenges.intro_fact: Good Friday in Ireland has traditionally meant fish instead of meat. Ireland has one of Europe's largest exclusive economic zones, yet imports most of its seafood while exporting much of what it catches.

questions.text: What percentage of the world's fish stocks are currently overfished or fished at maximum capacity?
questions.fact: Over 90% of global fish stocks are now fully or over-exploited, according to the FAO. That's up from 10% in the 1970s — a dramatic shift in just 50 years.

questions.text: Which of these fish is considered a more sustainable choice in Irish waters?
questions.fact: Mackerel is one of the more sustainable choices in Irish waters — it's abundant, low in the food chain and caught without destructive methods.

questions.text: How much CO₂ does a portion of farmed salmon produce compared to a portion of chicken?
questions.fact: Farmed salmon produces roughly twice the CO₂ of chicken per kg — mainly because of the energy-intensive feed. Wild-caught small fish like mackerel or sardines are far lower.

challenges.action_intro: The sea gives Ireland a lot — coastline, food, tourism and identity. Looking after it starts with what we put on our plates.

actions.title: Check the sustainability rating of your fish today
actions.desc: The Good Fish Guide by the Marine Conservation Society rates fish by sustainability. Check goodfishguide.org before you buy fish this week.

actions.title: Try mackerel, mussels or sardines this week
actions.desc: These are among the most sustainable and nutritious seafood options in Ireland — and usually cheaper than salmon or tuna. Tinned works just as well.

challenges.intro_fact: April is when Ireland comes alive. Over 11,000 species of plants and animals are found in Ireland — and spring is the busiest season for most of them. But biodiversity has declined significantly over the past 50 years, largely due to changes in farming.

questions.text: What proportion of Ireland's land is covered by peatland (bog)?
questions.fact: About 20% of Ireland's land area is peatland — one of the highest proportions in Europe. Intact bogs store enormous amounts of carbon but have been heavily damaged by drainage and peat cutting.

questions.text: Which Irish habitat has seen the steepest decline in recent decades?
questions.fact: Raised bogs have lost over 90% of their natural condition in Ireland. They are slow to form — some are 10,000 years old — and almost impossible to fully restore once drained.

questions.text: How many species of wild bee are found in Ireland?
questions.fact: Ireland has around 100 species of wild bee, including 20 bumblebee species. One third of these are threatened with extinction — mainly due to loss of flower-rich habitats and pesticide use.

challenges.action_intro: Ireland's biodiversity is genuinely special — but it is under pressure. The good news is that gardens, balconies and even window boxes can play a real role.

actions.title: Download the iNaturalist app and log one species this week
actions.desc: iNaturalist is free and lets you photograph plants, birds or insects and have them identified automatically. Every observation contributes to national biodiversity data.

actions.title: Plant one native Irish wildflower this spring
actions.desc: Primrose, cowslip, wild garlic or ox-eye daisy are all easy to grow in pots or gardens and support native insects. Most garden centres stock them from April.

challenges.intro_fact: Ireland gets plenty of rain — but that doesn't mean we're off the hook on water. The average Irish person uses about 150 litres of water per day at home, but their total water footprint including food and products is closer to 4,000 litres a day.

questions.text: How many litres of water does it take to produce 1 kg of beef?
questions.fact: 1 kg of beef requires roughly 15,000 litres of water — most of it for growing the feed crops. That's about 100 showers worth for a single kilo of meat.

questions.text: Which product uses more water to produce — a cotton T-shirt or a litre of wine?
options: A litre of wine uses more
questions.fact: A cotton T-shirt takes about 2,700 litres of water to produce — equivalent to roughly 3 years of drinking water for one person.

questions.text: What is the main water-related environmental problem facing Irish rivers right now?
questions.fact: Agricultural runoff — carrying excess nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilisers and slurry — is the leading cause of poor water quality in Irish rivers. Only 53% of Irish water bodies are in good ecological status.

challenges.action_intro: Water is easy to take for granted in Ireland — but the water embedded in our food and clothes is a global issue. Farmers in water-stressed regions grow the crops that end up on our plates.

actions.title: Fix a dripping tap at home this week
actions.desc: A dripping tap wastes up to 15 litres a day — that's over 5,000 litres a year. Most fixes take 10 minutes and cost very little.

actions.title: Eat one less portion of beef this week
actions.desc: Replacing one beef meal with chicken, fish or legumes saves not just carbon but a significant amount of embedded water.

challenges.intro_fact: April is one of the best months to spot Ireland's wildflowers. Hedgerows are one of Ireland's most important habitats, home to over 80% of our mammal species, most of our breeding birds, and thousands of insects.

questions.text: How many kilometres of hedgerow does Ireland have?
questions.fact: Ireland has approximately 700,000 km of hedgerows — more per square kilometre than almost any other country in Europe. They are a uniquely Irish habitat and a vital carbon store.

questions.text: What is the main threat to Irish hedgerows right now?
questions.fact: Agricultural removal and mechanical cutting — often outside the legal cutting season — are the main threats. It's illegal to cut hedges between 1 March and 31 August to protect nesting birds.

questions.text: Which common Irish wildflower is one of the best early-season food sources for bees?
questions.fact: Gorse (furze) flowers almost year-round and is one of the most important early nectar sources for bumblebees in Ireland. There's an old Irish saying: 'When gorse is out of bloom, kissing is out of season.'

challenges.action_intro: Ireland's wild landscape is shaped by its hedgerows, bogs and coastal habitats. Getting to know them is the first step to caring about them.

actions.title: Go for a hedgerow walk and identify 3 species
actions.desc: Use the free iNaturalist or PlantNet app to identify what's growing in a local hedgerow. Hawthorn, blackthorn and elder are the most common in Ireland.

actions.title: Plant a native Irish hedgerow plant in your garden
actions.desc: Hawthorn, blackthorn or hazel are all cheap, fast-growing and excellent for wildlife. Even a single plant in a garden makes a difference for birds and insects.

challenges.intro_fact: In Ireland, 1 in 4 people will experience a mental health difficulty at some point. Yet one of the most effective interventions is also the most underused: spending time in nature. The science behind 'green prescribing' is growing fast.

questions.text: By how much can a 90-minute walk in nature reduce activity in the brain area linked to negative thinking?
questions.fact: Stanford researchers found that a 90-minute walk in nature significantly reduced neural activity in the prefrontal cortex — the area linked to rumination and anxiety.

questions.text: What is 'green prescribing' as used in Irish healthcare?
options: GPs recommending nature-based activities instead of or alongside medication
A government scheme to plant trees near hospitals
questions.fact: Green prescribing involves GPs recommending nature-based activities — walking, gardening, birdwatching — as part of treatment for anxiety, depression and loneliness. It is growing across Irish primary care.

questions.text: Which Irish programme connects people with mental health difficulties to outdoor nature activities?
questions.fact: Green Care Ireland connects people experiencing mental health and social difficulties with therapeutic nature-based activities — farming, gardening, animal care and conservation work.

challenges.action_intro: Mental health and the environment are deeply connected. When we look after nature, it looks after us — and the evidence for this is stronger than ever.

actions.title: Take a 20-minute walk outside without your phone this week
actions.desc: Leave the podcast and headphones behind just once. Walk somewhere green if you can — a park, a canal path, a beach. Notice what you see, hear and smell.

actions.title: Suggest a walking meeting at work this week
actions.desc: Replace one sit-down meeting with a walk-and-talk outside. It's better for creativity, better for wellbeing, and uses no energy.

challenges.intro_fact: Ireland has one of the most vibrant live music scenes in the world. A single large music festival can produce over 500 tonnes of CO₂ — mainly from travel, generators and single-use waste. More festivals are now trying to change that.

questions.text: What proportion of a typical music festival's carbon footprint comes from audience travel?
questions.fact: Up to 80% of a festival's total carbon footprint comes from how the audience gets there. Encouraging public transport, carpooling and cycling can make a huge difference.

questions.text: Which Irish festival was among the first in Europe to introduce a reusable cup system?
questions.fact: Electric Picnic introduced a reusable cup system early on. Body & Soul has also been a pioneer — running on 100% renewable energy.

questions.text: How much waste does the average festival-goer generate per day?
questions.fact: Festival-goers generate around 3 kg of waste per day — roughly 3x the daily average at home. Much of that is avoidable: food packaging, single-use cups, and abandoned tents.

challenges.action_intro: Festivals are one of the great joys of Irish summer — and the industry is changing fast. Our choices around travel and waste are the two biggest levers we have.

actions.title: If you're going to a festival this summer, plan to travel by public transport
actions.desc: Most major Irish festivals are served by shuttle buses or trains. Check the transport options now and book early — it's usually cheaper and takes the parking stress away.
actions.carbon: Could save 20–50 kg CO₂ vs driving alone

actions.title: Pack a festival kit that cuts waste
actions.desc: Reusable cup, water bottle, solid shampoo bar, and a bag for sorting recycling. Most of this costs nothing if you already have it.

challenges.intro_fact: Ireland has one of the richest marine environments in Europe. The Shannon Estuary has one of the only resident bottlenose dolphin populations in Europe, and Irish waters are home to over 25 species of whales and dolphins.

questions.text: What percentage of the world's oxygen is produced by ocean phytoplankton?
questions.fact: About 50% of the world's oxygen is produced by marine phytoplankton. The ocean also absorbs around 25% of our CO₂ emissions each year, making it our biggest climate ally.

questions.text: What is the main threat to the Shannon Estuary dolphins today?
options: Boat disturbance, pollution and fishing bycatch
questions.fact: The Shannon dolphins face multiple threats: boat disturbance, marine pollution, and accidental capture in fishing nets (bycatch). The population of around 115 animals is considered vulnerable.

questions.text: How much plastic enters the world's oceans every year?
questions.fact: Around 8 million tonnes of plastic enters the ocean every year — equivalent to a rubbish truck emptying into the sea every minute.

challenges.action_intro: Ireland's ocean is one of our greatest natural assets — and it is under real pressure from plastic, pollution and climate change. What we do on land ends up in the sea.

actions.title: Take part in a Clean Coasts beach clean this month
actions.desc: Clean Coasts Ireland runs regular community beach cleans around the whole coast. Find one at cleancoasts.org — they provide bags and gloves.

actions.title: Switch to a plastic-free shampoo or soap bar
actions.desc: Shampoo bars last 2–3x longer than bottled versions and avoid the plastic entirely. Several Irish brands now make them.

challenges.intro_fact: Today is World Art Day. Climate grief, hope and action are increasingly central themes in Irish art — from theatre to visual art to music. Can culture change minds where facts can't?

questions.text: Research on climate communication suggests which approach is most effective at motivating behaviour change?
options: Stories of real people making positive change
questions.fact: Narrative and personal stories are consistently more effective than data or fear-based messaging at motivating action. People connect with people — not with statistics.

questions.text: What is 'solastalgia' — a term increasingly used in climate discussions?
options: Grief for environmental changes in one's home place
The mental health benefit of nature
questions.fact: Solastalgia describes the emotional distress caused by environmental change in one's home environment. It's increasingly recognised in Irish farming and coastal communities facing climate change.

questions.text: Which of these describes the relationship between Irish culture and the natural world?
options: Largely separate — Irish culture is urban
Historically close — land, bog and coast run through Irish writing and art
Only recently connected through climate activism
questions.fact: Land, bog, coast and seasons run through Irish writing and art — from Seamus Heaney's bogs to contemporary climate artists. Nature and Irish cultural identity have always been closely intertwined.

challenges.action_intro: Facts inform. Stories move people to act. That's why art, games, music and storytelling are not extras in the climate conversation — they are central to it.

actions.title: Find one piece of art, music or writing about nature or climate this week
actions.desc: A poem, a documentary, an album, a painting — it doesn't matter. Notice how it makes you feel. Art reaches the parts that facts sometimes can't.
actions.carbon: Builds emotional connection to the issue

actions.title: Support an Irish environmental arts project
actions.desc: Look up Commonage, Phizzfest or similar Irish environmental arts programmes. Even sharing their work on social media helps build the audience for climate culture.

challenges.intro_fact: 42% of Irish people say they feel lectured when climate topics come up — and that stops the conversation before it starts. Learning to talk about climate in a way that connects rather than alienates is one of the most useful skills you can develop.

questions.text: According to research, what is the most effective opening for a climate conversation?
options: Ask what they care about and connect it to climate
Tell them what changes they need to make
questions.fact: Starting with shared values — not climate facts — is the most effective approach. If someone cares about their children's health, or their local landscape, those are the doors into the conversation.

questions.text: What percentage of people globally are worried about climate change but rarely discuss it?
questions.fact: Research by Yale found that around 60–65% of people are worried about climate change but rarely talk about it — creating a 'spiral of silence' where everyone thinks they are in the minority.

questions.text: The '25% tipping point' theory suggests social norms shift when what proportion of a community commits to a new behaviour?
questions.fact: Research backed by the IPCC shows just 10–25% of committed individuals can shift a social norm for the whole group. You don't need everyone — just enough people willing to act visibly.

challenges.action_intro: Most people want to do more — they just don't know how to start. Talking openly and without judgement is one of the most powerful things any of us can do.

actions.title: Have one climate conversation this week — without lecturing
actions.desc: Start by asking someone what they think about something local — the weather, food prices, a nature story in the news. Listen first. Share one surprising fact if it feels natural.

actions.title: Share one thing you learned today on social media or WhatsApp
actions.desc: Even a short message or forwarding this quiz to one person breaks the spiral of silence. You don't need to be an expert — just curious.

challenges.intro_fact: Today is World Creativity and Innovation Day. Ireland has quietly become a hub for clean tech — from offshore wind potential to green hydrogen research. Ireland has enough offshore wind resource to power the country several times over.

questions.text: What percentage of Ireland's electricity came from renewable sources in 2024?
questions.fact: In 2024, around 60% of Ireland's electricity came from renewables — mainly wind power. Ireland's target is 80% by 2030, one of the more ambitious in Europe.

questions.text: Ireland's offshore wind resource is estimated to be how many times larger than its current electricity demand?
questions.fact: Ireland's offshore wind resource has been estimated at more than 10 times its current electricity demand — potentially making Ireland a major exporter of clean energy to Europe.

questions.text: What is 'green hydrogen' and why is it relevant to Ireland?
options: Hydrogen made using excess wind energy — Ireland has several projects underway
A government grant for home heating
A new type of solar panel technology
questions.fact: Green hydrogen is made by using surplus wind electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. Ireland's windy west coast makes it well placed to produce green hydrogen for export to Europe.

challenges.action_intro: Ireland's clean energy story is one of the most exciting in Europe — and the transition creates jobs, cuts bills and reduces our dependence on imported fossil fuels.

actions.title: Check if your home energy provider offers a green tariff
actions.desc: Many Irish energy suppliers now offer tariffs where your electricity is matched to renewable generation. Switching can take less than 10 minutes online.

actions.title: Look into the SEAI home retrofit grant scheme
actions.desc: The SEAI offers grants of up to €25,000 for home insulation, heat pumps and solar panels. Even reading through the options at seai.ie is a useful first step.
actions.carbon: Potential to cut home emissions by 50–70%

challenges.intro_fact: Earth Day is celebrated every year on 22 April by over 1 billion people in 193 countries. It was first held in 1970 and led directly to the creation of the US Environmental Protection Agency.

questions.text: What percentage of Irish people say they are willing to make some changes to address climate change?
questions.fact: 80% of Irish people say they are willing to make some changes — but only 16% believe they personally should be doing more. That gap is the challenge Environmentle is designed to help close.

questions.text: What share of total greenhouse gas emissions worldwide is linked to household behaviour?
questions.fact: 72% of all global greenhouse gas emissions can be traced back to household consumption — energy, food, transport and goods. Individual choices, multiplied across millions, are not small.

questions.text: Research suggests that once what proportion of a population commits to a new norm, it can spread to the rest?
questions.fact: The 25% Revolution, backed by IPCC research, shows that shifting a social norm only requires 10–25% of individuals to be deeply committed. Your actions influence the people around you.

challenges.action_intro: Earth Day is a moment to reflect and act. Small individual actions, multiplied across millions of people, genuinely add up. You don't need to fix everything — just do your bit.

actions.title: Calculate your carbon footprint today
actions.desc: Use a free online calculator — try myclimate.org or the WWF footprint calculator. It takes 5 minutes and shows where your biggest impact areas are.

actions.title: Commit to one meat-free day per week
actions.desc: Switching one day per week from meat to plant-based food is one of the highest-impact individual diet changes. Try it for April first.

actions.title: Talk to 3 people about climate action this week
actions.desc: Share what you learned today. Research shows social norms shift when people talk openly about behaviour change — and most people are more open than you'd expect.

challenges.intro_fact: Today is UNESCO World Book Day. Reading is one of the most effective ways to shift perspective — and the quality of climate writing has never been better. From hopeful rewilding books to page-turning climate science, there is something for everyone.

questions.text: Which book ranked reducing food waste and a plant-rich diet higher than solar panels as climate solutions?
options: This Changes Everything by Naomi Klein
The Sixth Extinction by Elizabeth Kolbert
questions.fact: 'Drawdown' edited by Paul Hawken ranked the top 100 solutions to climate change by impact. Reducing food waste and a plant-rich diet ranked higher than solar panels — genuinely surprising.

questions.text: What does research say about people who read fiction about climate change?
options: They become more anxious and less likely to act
They show increased empathy and willingness to act
It has no measurable effect on attitudes
They focus on fictional solutions, not real ones
questions.fact: Studies show that reading climate fiction increases empathy for those affected and raises the likelihood of pro-environmental behaviour. Stories build the emotional connection that facts alone cannot.

questions.text: Which Irish or Ireland-connected writer is known for engaging with themes of nature, land and bog?
questions.fact: Seamus Heaney's poetry is deeply rooted in the Irish bogland and rural landscape — his work helped generations connect with the natural world and understand land as something precious and fragile.

challenges.action_intro: Understanding is the foundation of action — and there has never been more good reading, listening and watching available on climate and nature.

actions.title: Add one climate or nature book to your reading list
actions.desc: Try 'Braiding Sweetgrass' by Robin Wall Kimmerer, 'Feral' by George Monbiot, or 'How to Avoid a Climate Disaster' by Bill Gates. Your local library will likely have at least one.

actions.title: Listen to one episode of a climate or nature podcast this week
actions.desc: Try 'How to Save a Planet', 'Outrage + Optimism', or 'The Irish Times Climate Podcast'. Even one episode can shift how you think about the issue.

challenges.intro_fact: Ireland is one of the least forested countries in Europe — only about 11% of land is covered by trees, compared to an EU average of 38%. Most of that is commercial Sitka spruce. But native woodland is slowly recovering.

questions.text: What percentage of Ireland's land area is covered by native woodland?
questions.fact: Less than 1% of Ireland is covered by native woodland — one of the lowest in Europe. Once Ireland was covered in oak, ash and hazel. Most was cleared for farming and fuel over thousands of years.

questions.text: How much CO₂ can a single mature oak tree absorb per year?
questions.fact: A mature oak tree absorbs roughly 22 kg of CO₂ per year. The real carbon value of forests comes from the soil beneath them, which can store 3–5x more carbon than the trees themselves.

questions.text: What is Ireland's current target for forest cover by 2050?
questions.fact: Ireland's target is 18% forest cover by 2050 — still below the EU average, but a significant increase from today. Meeting it requires planting around 8,000 hectares per year, which Ireland is currently short of.

challenges.action_intro: Planting trees is not a silver bullet for climate change — but native woodland restoration is genuinely important for carbon, biodiversity and water quality in Ireland. Every tree helps.

actions.title: Plant a tree — or fund one being planted
actions.desc: Native Irish trees like oak, birch, hazel or rowan. If you don't have a garden, organisations like Easy Treesie or Native Woodland Trust plant on your behalf.

actions.title: Choose wood products with FSC certification
actions.desc: The Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) label means timber came from responsibly managed forests. Look for it on paper, furniture and wood products — widely available in Irish shops.

challenges.intro_fact: Ireland generates about 14 million tonnes of waste every year — one of the highest per-capita rates in Europe. Most of that is avoidable. The circular economy is about designing waste out from the start.

questions.text: What percentage of materials that enter the global economy are still in use 6 months after purchase?
questions.fact: The Ellen MacArthur Foundation found that only about 9% of materials that enter the global economy are still in productive use 6 months later. The rest ends up in landfill, incineration or stockpiles.

questions.text: Which of these is the most effective waste reduction strategy according to the waste hierarchy?
questions.fact: The waste hierarchy puts refusal and reduction at the top — the best waste is waste that was never created. Recycling is near the bottom; it still uses energy and creates emissions.

questions.text: What does the EU Right to Repair directive require from manufacturers?
options: All products must come with a 10-year warranty
Manufacturers must provide spare parts and repair services for common products
All electronics must be repairable by the consumer
Products must be made from 50% recycled materials
questions.fact: The EU Right to Repair directive requires manufacturers of certain products — white goods, electronics, smartphones — to provide spare parts, repair manuals and repair services for a set number of years after sale.

challenges.action_intro: The most sustainable product is the one you already own. Before buying anything new this week, ask: can I borrow it, repair it, or buy it second-hand?

actions.title: Repair something instead of replacing it this week
actions.desc: A torn bag, a broken button, a cracked phone case — look up a repair tutorial before buying a replacement. Repair Cafés operate in most Irish cities and are free to attend.
actions.carbon: Extends product life, avoids manufacturing emissions

actions.title: Declutter one drawer or shelf and donate or sell what you don't use
actions.desc: Donating to charity shops, selling on Done Deal or giving away on Buy Nothing groups keeps items in circulation and out of landfill.

challenges.intro_fact: Today is World Day for Safety and Health at Work. Burnout costs Irish businesses an estimated €1.5 billion per year in lost productivity. Workplaces with stronger sustainability cultures tend to have higher employee wellbeing and lower turnover.

questions.text: What percentage of Irish workers say they would prefer to work for a company with strong environmental values?
questions.fact: Surveys consistently show around 65–70% of workers — rising to over 80% among under-35s — prefer to work for companies with genuine sustainability commitments.

questions.text: Which workplace intervention has the strongest evidence for improving employee wellbeing?
options: Access to natural light and greenery
questions.fact: Access to natural light and indoor plants consistently ranks among the strongest predictors of workplace wellbeing — yet most Irish office environments still underinvest in it.

questions.text: What does 'scope 3 emissions' mean in a workplace context?
options: Emissions from employee commuting and the supply chain
Emissions outside a company's legal obligation
questions.fact: Scope 3 emissions cover indirect emissions — including employee commuting, business travel, and the supply chain. For most Irish businesses, these represent 70–90% of their total carbon footprint.

challenges.action_intro: Workplace sustainability and employee wellbeing go hand in hand — and Irish businesses are starting to take both seriously. You don't need to be the CEO to start a conversation about it.

actions.title: Suggest one green initiative at your workplace this week
actions.desc: It could be as simple as asking about switching to a green energy tariff, starting a composting scheme, or setting up a lunchtime walking group.

actions.title: Swap one car commute for walking, cycling or public transport
actions.desc: Even one day per week makes a difference. Most Irish cities now have Bike to Work schemes and Leap card subsidies through employers.

challenges.intro_fact: Today is Stop Food Waste Day. Irish households throw away an estimated €700 worth of food every year — that's about €60 a month per family. Food waste in Ireland produces around 1.6 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent annually. Most of it is completely avoidable.

questions.text: What percentage of all food produced globally is wasted?
questions.fact: Roughly one third of all food produced globally is lost or wasted. If food waste were a country, it would be the third largest emitter of greenhouse gases in the world.

questions.text: Which food category is most wasted in Irish homes?
questions.fact: Fresh fruit and vegetables are the most wasted food category in Irish homes, followed by bread. Most happens because people buy more than they need or don't use produce before it goes off.

questions.text: According to Project Drawdown, reducing food waste is ranked how among all climate solutions?
questions.fact: Reducing food waste ranks in the top 5 climate solutions globally according to Project Drawdown — higher than solar panels, electric vehicles or wind power.

challenges.action_intro: Wasting less food is one of the single highest-impact climate actions you can take — and it saves you money at the same time. A weekly meal plan and a fridge check before shopping are all it takes to start.

actions.title: Do a fridge audit before your next food shop
actions.desc: Before you go shopping this week, check what's already in your fridge and cupboards. Write a list based on what you actually need. Stick to it.

actions.title: Try one 'use it up' meal this week
actions.desc: Cook one meal entirely from what's already in the fridge and cupboards — no new shopping. It's often surprisingly good and saves money and waste.

actions.title: Download the Too Good To Go app
actions.desc: Too Good To Go lets you buy surplus food from local restaurants, cafés and supermarkets at a fraction of the price. Available in Dublin, Cork, Galway and many other Irish towns.

challenges.intro_fact: We talk a lot about carbon and plastic — but pollution comes in many forms. Noise pollution, light pollution and air quality are all significant environmental health issues in Irish cities, and all are linked to climate-related choices like transport and energy.

questions.text: According to the WHO, noise pollution is the second largest environmental health risk in Europe after what?
questions.fact: The WHO identifies noise pollution as the second largest environmental health risk in Europe after air pollution, linked to cardiovascular disease, sleep disruption and cognitive impairment.

questions.text: What percentage of Irish people are exposed to road traffic noise above EU recommended levels?
questions.fact: Around 30% of Irish people are exposed to road traffic noise above EU recommended levels — with the highest exposure in Dublin, Cork and Limerick city centres.

questions.text: How did reduced car traffic during COVID-19 lockdowns affect bird biodiversity in cities?
options: Slightly negative — birds use road noise as navigation
Significantly positive — more species and more complex birdsong
Mixed results depending on the city
questions.fact: Studies found that reducing traffic noise led to significantly richer birdsong — more species, more complex songs, and birds able to communicate over longer distances.

challenges.action_intro: Pollution isn't always visible. Noise, light and air quality all affect our health and the health of wildlife around us — and many of the fixes are the same: fewer cars, more green space, cleaner energy.

actions.title: Create a quiet hour at home this evening — no screens, no background noise
actions.desc: Turn off the TV and music for one hour. Read, cook, chat or sit outside. Notice how your body responds to the quiet.

actions.title: Walk or cycle instead of driving for one short trip this week
actions.desc: Every car journey replaced by walking or cycling removes noise, reduces air pollution, cuts carbon and is good for your health.

challenges.intro_fact: Ireland has one of the lowest cycling rates in Europe for commuting. Only about 3% of Irish workers cycle to work, despite most urban commutes being under 5km. That is starting to change — but slowly.

questions.text: What is the most common reason Irish people give for not cycling to work?
questions.fact: Weather is cited most often — yet Copenhagen and Amsterdam have similar climates and much higher cycling rates. The difference is infrastructure and habit.

questions.text: How much CO₂ does replacing one 5km car commute with cycling save per year?
questions.fact: Cycling instead of driving 5km each way, 5 days a week saves roughly 300 kg of CO₂ per year — the equivalent of planting around 15 trees.

questions.text: Ireland's Bike to Work scheme lets employees buy a bike tax-free up to what value?
questions.fact: Since 2022, the Bike to Work scheme covers up to €3,000 for cargo bikes and e-bikes. Standard bikes are covered up to €1,500. The scheme saves up to 52% on the cost.

challenges.action_intro: Most Irish commutes are short enough to cycle — but infrastructure and habit are the barriers. One change a week builds momentum faster than you think.

actions.title: Check if your employer is signed up to the Bike to Work scheme
actions.desc: Visit biketowork.ie — it takes 5 minutes. The scheme saves you up to 52% on a new bike through salary sacrifice.

actions.title: Try cycling or walking for one short trip this week instead of driving
actions.desc: Any trip under 3km is faster by bike in most Irish towns once you factor in parking. Give it one try this week.

challenges.resources: Bike to Work scheme: biketowork.ie | Irish cycling news and advocacy: irishcycle.com | European Cyclists' Federation: ecf.com | NTA cycling maps: nta.ie

challenges.intro_fact: Ireland has one of the highest rates of asthma in Europe — affecting around 1 in 13 people. Air quality is directly linked to how we heat our homes and how we travel. Most Irish homes still rely on oil or solid fuel — two of the most polluting heating options available.

questions.text: What is the main cause of poor air quality in Irish towns and villages in winter?
questions.fact: Smoky coal and wet wood burned in open fireplaces is the leading cause of particulate air pollution in Irish towns in winter. The national smoky coal ban, extended in 2022, has made a measurable difference.

questions.text: What is the most common home heating system in rural Ireland?
questions.fact: Around 40% of Irish homes use oil as their primary heating source, rising to over 60% in rural areas. Oil heating produces roughly 3x more CO₂ than a modern heat pump running on Irish grid electricity.

questions.text: What does the EU Green Deal commit Europe to by 2050?
options: Becoming the world's first climate-neutral continent
Phasing out all fossil fuel imports
Planting 1 billion trees across member states
questions.fact: The EU Green Deal commits Europe to climate neutrality by 2050 — the most ambitious climate framework in the world. Ireland's Climate Action Plan sits within this legally binding framework.

challenges.action_intro: Home heating is the single biggest source of household emissions in Ireland — and the biggest opportunity. Even small steps like draught-proofing or switching fuel type make a real difference.

actions.title: Check your home's BER rating
actions.desc: Visit seai.ie — it is free and shows where you lose most heat and energy. A poor BER means higher bills and higher emissions.
actions.carbon: Awareness step — improving BER can cut emissions by up to 50%

actions.title: Look into the SEAI heat pump grant if you heat with oil
actions.desc: The SEAI grant covers up to €6,500 towards switching from oil to a heat pump. Visit seai.ie/grants — even reading the options is a useful first step.
actions.carbon: Switching from oil to heat pump saves ~2–3 tonnes CO₂ per year

challenges.resources: SEAI home energy grants: seai.ie/grants | EPA Ireland air quality data: epa.ie/our-services/monitoring--assessment/air | EU Green Deal: ec.europa.eu/clima/eu-action/european-green-deal | Asthma Society of Ireland: asthma.ie

challenges.intro_fact: The traditional Irish diet — potatoes, oats, vegetables, fish, a little dairy — was actually one of the lowest-carbon diets in Europe. The shift to highly processed food and more meat has significantly increased Ireland's food-related emissions over the past 50 years.

questions.text: Which traditional Irish food has the lowest carbon footprint?
questions.fact: Potatoes and cabbage are both low-carbon, low-water crops grown easily in Ireland's climate. Colcannon is as Irish as it gets — and one of the most sustainable meals on the menu.

questions.text: How much more carbon does 1 kg of Irish beef produce compared to 1 kg of potatoes?
questions.fact: Beef produces roughly 60 kg CO₂ per kg of food. Potatoes produce around 1.2 kg — about 50x less. Ireland's beef sector is world-class in quality but its climate footprint is significant.

questions.text: What Irish word, increasingly used in climate and heritage policy, describes the deep connection between people and their local landscape?
questions.fact: Dúchas means heritage, nature and a sense of belonging to a place. It is used in Irish environmental policy to describe the relationship between communities and the natural landscape they depend on.

challenges.action_intro: The food on our plates is one of the most direct connections we have to the land, the climate and the culture around us. Small switches made consistently add up to a real impact.

actions.title: Cook one traditional Irish plant-based meal this week
actions.desc: Colcannon, vegetable soup, or oat porridge — simple, cheap and very low carbon. The traditional Irish diet was ahead of its time.
actions.carbon: Plant-based meals save 1–3 kg CO₂ vs meat equivalent

actions.title: Buy one Irish-grown vegetable this week instead of an imported one
actions.desc: Check the label — Irish-grown carrots, cabbage, leeks and potatoes are widely available in all supermarkets. Supporting local reduces food miles and keeps Irish farming land productive.
actions.carbon: Reduces food miles and supports Irish land use

challenges.resources: Our World in Data — food emissions: ourworldindata.org/food-choice-vs-eating-local | Teagasc food and farming: teagasc.ie | Bord Bia Irish food: bordbia.ie | Irish Seed Savers: irishseedsavers.ie

challenges.intro_fact: Ireland has over 3,000 km of waymarked trails — yet most Irish people rarely use them. Regular outdoor exercise is one of the most effective ways to both improve personal wellbeing and build a lasting connection to nature. You cannot protect what you do not know.

questions.text: How much time outdoors per week is linked to significantly better mental and physical health, according to research?
questions.fact: Spending at least 2 hours per week in nature is linked to significantly better health and wellbeing — even in short visits spread across the week. The effect holds for people of all ages and backgrounds.

questions.text: What percentage of Irish people say they do not have easy access to a safe outdoor space for exercise near their home?
questions.fact: Access to green space and safe outdoor areas is very unequal in Ireland — particularly in disadvantaged urban areas and rural communities without footpaths or safe roads.

questions.text: Ireland's National Trails Office is part of which organisation?
questions.fact: The National Trails Office manages Ireland's waymarked trail network under Sport Ireland. Trails range from short loop walks to multi-day routes like the Wicklow Way and the Wild Atlantic Way.

challenges.action_intro: Moving outside is good for your body, your mind and your connection to the natural world. It costs nothing and is available to most people — even in cities.

actions.title: Plan one outdoor walk this weekend using the Trails Ireland app
actions.desc: The Trails Ireland app is free and lists thousands of walks across the country by location, distance and difficulty. Find one near you and go.

actions.title: Swap one gym session for an outdoor run or walk this week
actions.desc: Outdoor exercise has been shown to have greater mental health benefits than the same exercise indoors — and it uses no energy.
actions.carbon: Saves gym energy use + connects you to local nature

challenges.resources: National Trails Office: sportireland.ie/trails | Trails Ireland app: trailsireland.ie | Leave No Trace Ireland: leavenotraceireland.org | Green Care Ireland: greencareireland.ie

challenges.intro_fact: During WWII, Irish households repaired everything, wasted almost nothing, and grew food in every available space. The average wartime diet produced a fraction of today's carbon footprint — not by choice, but by necessity. What can we borrow from that mindset today?

questions.text: What was the name of the Irish government initiative during WWII that encouraged people to grow their own food?
questions.fact: During 'The Emergency' — Ireland's term for WWII — the government encouraged food growing on any available land. Allotments, school gardens and park plots all contributed to local food supply.

questions.text: How much food waste did the average Irish household produce during wartime rationing compared to today?
questions.fact: Rationing meant every scrap of food had a value. Bread crusts, vegetable peelings and leftovers were all reused. The contrast with today — where Irish households waste an estimated €700 of food per year — is striking.

questions.text: The repair economy in Ireland during WWII was driven by necessity. What EU law is now bringing this approach back?
options: The EU Right to Repair Directive
questions.fact: The EU Right to Repair Directive (2024) requires manufacturers to make common products repairable and to provide spare parts. Ireland is already implementing it — a legal return to the wartime mindset of fix before replace.

challenges.action_intro: The habits that made wartime households more resilient are the same ones that make us more sustainable today — less waste, more repair, more local food. None of them require sacrifice.

actions.title: Repair something this week instead of replacing it
actions.desc: A torn bag, a broken button, a cracked phone case — look up a repair tutorial on YouTube before buying a replacement. Repair Cafés operate in most Irish cities and are free. Find one at repaircafe.ie.
actions.carbon: Extends product life and avoids manufacturing emissions

actions.title: Cook one meal entirely from what is already in your fridge and cupboards
actions.desc: Before your next shop, cook once using only what you already have. It is usually cheaper, wastes nothing and is often surprisingly good.
actions.carbon: Direct food waste reduction — saves ~€700/year if done regularly

challenges.resources: Repair Café Ireland: repaircafe.ie | Stop Food Waste Ireland: stopfoodwaste.ie | EU Right to Repair: ec.europa.eu | National Museum of Ireland — The Emergency: museum.ie

challenges.intro_fact: This week is Dublin Climate Action Week — a city-wide moment to reflect, learn and act. We kick it off with something that happens right above your head every spring. Over 70 species of migratory birds arrive in Ireland between March and May, travelling thousands of kilometres from Africa and southern Europe. Climate change is shifting their arrival times — and that has knock-on effects across entire ecosystems.

questions.text: Which of these birds migrates from West Africa to breed in Ireland every spring?
questions.fact: Swallows travel up to 10,000 km from Sub-Saharan Africa to breed in Ireland each spring. They typically arrive in April and leave again in September. Their numbers have declined by over 30% in Ireland since the 1980s.

questions.text: What is the main reason migratory bird populations are declining in Ireland?
options: Loss of insect food sources and nesting habitats
questions.fact: Intensive farming, pesticide use and habitat loss have dramatically reduced the insects that migratory birds depend on for food. No insects means no food for birds — even if they complete the journey successfully.

questions.text: Ireland is part of which major migratory bird flyway — the route birds use between breeding and wintering grounds?
questions.fact: The East Atlantic Flyway connects the Arctic and Western Europe with West Africa. Ireland is a critical stopping point — particularly for wading birds and seabirds — because of its position on the western edge of Europe.

challenges.action_intro: Birds are one of the best indicators of ecosystem health — and Ireland's declining farmland birds tell us something important about the state of our countryside. Small garden and outdoor changes genuinely help.

actions.title: Download the BirdWatch Ireland app and log one bird sighting this week
actions.desc: The app is free and lets you identify and record birds. Every sighting contributes to national population monitoring data used by scientists and policymakers.
actions.carbon: Supports citizen science and biodiversity monitoring

actions.title: Let a patch of your garden or outdoor space grow a little wilder this month
actions.desc: Stop cutting one corner of the lawn, or leave a strip along a fence uncut. Even small wild patches support the insects that birds — including migrants — depend on for food.
actions.carbon: Supports local insect and bird populations

challenges.resources: BirdWatch Ireland: birdwatchireland.ie | Dublin Climate Action Week: codema.ie | National Biodiversity Data Centre: biodiversityireland.ie | East Atlantic Flyway: wetlands.org

challenges.intro_fact: This week is Dublin Climate Action Week. Today we look at healthcare — an industry we rarely think of as a polluter. The global health sector is responsible for around 4.4% of total greenhouse gas emissions — more than aviation. In Ireland, the HSE has committed to reaching net zero by 2050, and green prescribing — where GPs recommend nature-based activities — is growing fast.

questions.text: What does the term 'green prescribing' mean?
options: Prescribing herbal medicines instead of pharmaceutical drugs
GPs recommending nature-based activities as part of treatment
A government scheme to plant trees near hospitals
Prescribing only medicines made from natural ingredients
questions.fact: Green prescribing involves doctors recommending activities like walking, gardening or birdwatching alongside or instead of medication for anxiety, depression and loneliness. It is growing across Irish primary care.

questions.text: What is the single largest source of emissions from the Irish health service?
questions.fact: The majority of the HSE's carbon footprint comes from its supply chain — including pharmaceuticals, equipment and food. This is a Scope 3 emissions challenge that is only beginning to be addressed.

questions.text: A single pressurised inhaler used for asthma produces roughly how much CO₂ equivalent?
options: About the same as boiling a kettle
About the same as a 10 km car journey
About the same as a 100 km car journey
About the same as a return flight to London
questions.fact: Pressurised metered-dose inhalers use hydrofluorocarbon propellants with a very high global warming potential. Switching to dry powder inhalers where clinically suitable can reduce this footprint by up to 90%.

challenges.action_intro: Healthcare and the environment are more connected than most people realise. The healthier our environment, the less pressure on our health system — and vice versa.

actions.title: Ask your GP about green prescribing or local nature-based wellbeing programmes
actions.desc: Look up local programmes at mentalhealthireland.ie or greencareireland.ie. Nature-based activities are increasingly recognised as effective treatment — not just lifestyle extras.
actions.carbon: Nature access is a public health issue

actions.title: Walk or cycle to your next GP or pharmacy visit if it is under 3 km
actions.desc: Short car trips under 3 km produce disproportionately high emissions per km because the engine never warms up fully. Walking or cycling is better for you and the air around the clinic.
actions.carbon: Short trips saved = disproportionate emissions reduction

challenges.resources: HSE Climate Action Strategy: hse.ie | Healthy Ireland: healthyireland.ie | Green Care Ireland: greencareireland.ie | Global health sector emissions: healthcareclimateaction.org

challenges.intro_fact: This week is Dublin Climate Action Week. Today we look at what is in your shopping basket. Ireland is one of the highest per-capita consumers of Fairtrade products in the world — but most people do not know what Fairtrade actually means for climate, or why it matters beyond ethics. Fairtrade farming practices often protect biodiversity and reduce deforestation.

questions.text: What does the Fairtrade mark on a product guarantee?
options: The product was made with zero carbon emissions
Farmers received a minimum price and investment in their communities
No pesticides were used in production
questions.fact: The Fairtrade mark guarantees producers a minimum price that covers the cost of sustainable production, plus a Fairtrade Premium invested in community projects like schools, healthcare and environmental protection.

questions.text: What is the main way dairy farming affects water quality in Irish rivers?
options: Fertiliser and slurry runoff carrying excess nutrients into waterways
questions.fact: Nutrient runoff from farms — particularly nitrogen and phosphorus — is the leading cause of poor water quality in Irish rivers. Only 53% of Irish water bodies currently meet good ecological status.

questions.text: Fairtrade certified farms are required to meet standards on which environmental practice?
options: Zero use of any chemical fertiliser
Prohibition of certain hazardous pesticides and protection of natural ecosystems
Mandatory carbon offsetting for all exports
questions.fact: Fairtrade environmental standards ban the most harmful pesticides, require protection of water sources and natural habitats. This makes Fairtrade relevant to biodiversity as well as ethics and fair pay.

challenges.action_intro: What we buy connects us directly to farming communities and ecosystems on the other side of the world. Fairtrade is not perfect — but it is one of the most accessible ways to make that connection a positive one.

actions.title: Swap one product in your weekly shop for a Fairtrade alternative
actions.desc: Coffee, tea, chocolate or bananas are the easiest starting points — all widely available in Irish supermarkets with the Fairtrade mark. Usually the same price or very close.
actions.carbon: Supports sustainable farming in climate-vulnerable regions

actions.title: Check if your workplace uses Fairtrade tea and coffee
actions.desc: If not, suggest it — it is usually the same price and some suppliers provide free point-of-sale materials. One workplace switch multiplies the effect across many people.

challenges.resources: Fairtrade Ireland: fairtrade.ie | Fairtrade International: fairtrade.net | Ethical Consumer guide: ethicalconsumer.org | Dublin Climate Action Week: codema.ie

challenges.intro_fact: This week is Dublin Climate Action Week. Today a slightly lighter hook — but a very real topic. Ireland has around 6.5 million cattle — more than its human population. Land use for livestock farming shapes almost everything about Ireland's landscape, water quality and emissions. How we farm is one of the biggest levers we have on climate and biodiversity.

questions.text: Roughly how much of Ireland's total land area is used for agriculture?
questions.fact: Around 70% of Ireland's land is used for agriculture — one of the highest proportions in Europe. The vast majority is permanent grassland for livestock. This shapes everything from biodiversity to water quality to carbon storage.

questions.text: What is the main greenhouse gas produced by Irish cattle, and how does it compare to CO₂?
options: CO₂ — same warming impact as other sectors
Methane — about 28x more potent than CO₂ over 100 years
Nitrous oxide — about 5x more potent than CO₂
Ammonia — the most potent agricultural gas
questions.fact: Irish cattle produce methane through digestion — called enteric fermentation. Methane is far more potent than CO₂ in the short term, which is why agriculture accounts for around 35% of Ireland's total greenhouse gas emissions.

questions.text: What is the name of the Irish government scheme that pays farmers to manage land in a way that benefits biodiversity and the environment?
questions.fact: ACRES (Agriculture Climate Rural Environment Scheme) pays Irish farmers for environmental actions — including protecting hedgerows, managing wetlands, reducing fertiliser use and supporting biodiversity. Over 50,000 farmers had applied by 2024.

challenges.action_intro: Irish farming is at a crossroads — under pressure to produce more while also reducing emissions and restoring biodiversity. Supporting farmers who are making that shift is something consumers and communities can do.

actions.title: Try one meal this week built around Irish-grown vegetables or legumes instead of meat
actions.desc: Legumes like lentils and beans fix nitrogen naturally, reducing the need for chemical fertiliser. They are cheap, filling and widely available. A simple dahl or bean stew works perfectly.
actions.carbon: Plant-based meals save 2–5 kg CO₂ vs beef equivalent

actions.title: Leave a corner of your outdoor space uncut this month
actions.desc: If you have a garden, leave one corner uncut until the end of May. Ground-nesting insects and small mammals use rough grass — and whatever flowers appear will support pollinators.
actions.carbon: Supports local insect and bird populations

challenges.resources: Teagasc — Irish farming and environment: teagasc.ie | ACRES scheme: gov.ie/agriculture | All-Ireland Pollinator Plan: pollinators.ie | EPA Ireland agriculture emissions: epa.ie

challenges.intro_fact: Today marks the end of Dublin Climate Action Week and the start of National Biodiversity Week across Ireland — with over 200 free events happening around the country. A good moment to think about the bigger picture. The average Irish household's carbon footprint is around 8 tonnes of CO₂ per year — but small changes across thousands of families add up fast.

questions.text: Which of these household actions saves the most CO₂ per year?
options: Switching off lights when leaving a room
Replacing a long-haul flight with a holiday in Ireland
Using a reusable coffee cup every day
questions.fact: Cutting one long-haul return flight saves roughly 1.5 to 3 tonnes of CO₂ — more than turning off every light in your home for a year. Aviation is one of the highest-impact areas for individual action.

questions.text: What percentage of a typical Irish family's carbon footprint comes from food choices?
questions.fact: Food accounts for roughly a quarter of a household's total carbon footprint — making it the second biggest area after home energy and transport. Reducing meat and dairy has the biggest single impact within that.

questions.text: Ireland's National Biodiversity Action Plan commits to protecting what percentage of Ireland's land and marine area by 2030?
questions.fact: Ireland has committed to protecting 30% of its land and marine area by 2030 — as part of the EU Biodiversity Strategy and the Global Kunming-Montreal framework. Ireland is currently far below that target.

challenges.action_intro: The environment is not separate from family life — it is the foundation of it. Clean air, safe water, access to nature and a stable climate are the things every family depends on.

actions.title: Visit one of Ireland's national parks or nature reserves this weekend
actions.desc: Ireland has 6 national parks — Killarney, Glenveagh, Connemara, Ballycroy, The Burren and Wicklow Mountains. All are free to enter. Find events near you at biodiversityweek.ie.
actions.carbon: Zero carbon + builds connection to nature

actions.title: Calculate your household carbon footprint together
actions.desc: Use the free calculator at myclimate.org — it takes about 10 minutes as a family and shows clearly where your biggest impact areas are. Knowing is the first step.

challenges.resources: National Biodiversity Week events: biodiversityweek.ie | National Parks and Wildlife Service: npws.ie | Household carbon calculator: myclimate.org | Dublin Climate Action Week wrap-up: codema.ie

challenges.intro_fact: It is National Biodiversity Week across Ireland — with over 200 free events happening around the country. Today, on International Museum Day, we focus on something simple but powerful: you cannot protect what you do not know. Ireland has extraordinary biodiversity — but most people could not name five wild plants or insects they pass every day.

questions.text: How many species of plants, animals and fungi are found in Ireland?
questions.fact: Ireland is home to around 11,000 recorded species — from lichens on rocks to whales off the west coast. Many are under threat. The National Biodiversity Data Centre tracks them all and relies partly on records from the public.

questions.text: What percentage of Ireland's assessed species are currently considered threatened or near threatened?
questions.fact: Around 20% of Ireland's assessed species are threatened or near threatened — including one third of wild bee species and many farmland birds. Habitat loss and intensive farming are the main drivers.

questions.text: Which Irish museum holds one of the largest natural history collections in Europe, with over 2 million specimens?
questions.fact: Known locally as the Dead Zoo, the Natural History Museum on Merrion Street holds over 2 million specimens and is one of the most intact Victorian natural history museums in the world. Entry is free.

challenges.action_intro: Ireland's biodiversity is genuinely special — and genuinely under pressure. Getting to know the nature around you is the first and most important step. Everything else follows from that.

actions.title: Download the free iNaturalist app and photograph one plant, bird or insect this week
actions.desc: iNaturalist identifies species from photos automatically and submits your record to national biodiversity databases. Every observation matters — especially outside the main cities.

actions.title: Check what biodiversity events are happening near you this week
actions.desc: Visit biodiversityweek.ie — events range from rockpool tours to moth nights to wildflower walks. Most are free and run by local naturalists, conservation groups and councils.
actions.carbon: Builds knowledge and local connection to nature

challenges.resources: National Biodiversity Week: biodiversityweek.ie | National Biodiversity Data Centre: biodiversityireland.ie | iNaturalist Ireland: inaturalist.org | Natural History Museum Dublin: museum.ie/natural-history

challenges.intro_fact: It is National Biodiversity Week. Today we look at one of the most debated food choices in Ireland. Dairy farming is central to Irish agriculture and culture — and also one of the biggest drivers of biodiversity loss through habitat conversion, fertiliser runoff and hedgerow removal. Ireland has over 1.4 million dairy cows. Bord Bia's Origin Green programme — Ireland's national food sustainability scheme — aims to make this sector more accountable. But how much progress is actually being made?

questions.text: Which plant milk has the lowest overall environmental footprint when you consider carbon, water and land use together?
questions.fact: Oat milk produces around 80% less CO₂ than cow's milk, uses far less water than almond milk and requires less land than soy. Oats also grow well in Irish and European climates, reducing food miles.

questions.text: What is the main way dairy farming affects water quality in Irish rivers?
options: Fertiliser and slurry runoff carrying excess nutrients into waterways
questions.fact: Nutrient runoff from dairy farms — particularly nitrogen and phosphorus — is the leading cause of poor water quality in Irish rivers. Only 53% of Irish water bodies currently meet good ecological status.

questions.text: Bord Bia's Origin Green is Ireland's national food sustainability programme. What percentage of Irish food and drink exports does it now cover?
questions.fact: Origin Green requires food businesses to set and report against sustainability targets covering carbon, water, biodiversity and social criteria. Over 90% of Irish food and drink exports are now covered — though critics note the programme is partly self-assessed.

challenges.action_intro: The food choices we make as consumers directly influence how Irish land is managed — and what lives on it. Small switches, made consistently, send real market signals.

actions.title: Try oat milk in your tea or coffee once this week
actions.desc: Irish brand Flahavan's now produces oat milk made from Irish-grown oats. One switch per day over a year saves roughly 50 to 100 kg CO₂. Most cafés and supermarkets stock it.
actions.carbon: ~50–100 kg CO₂ saved per year if switched daily

actions.title: If you buy dairy, look for the Origin Green or organic label
actions.desc: Both indicate higher environmental standards. Organic dairy farms support significantly more biodiversity than conventional farms — more wildflowers, more insects, more birds.
actions.carbon: Organic dairy supports significantly higher on-farm biodiversity

challenges.resources: Our World in Data food emissions: ourworldindata.org/food-choice-vs-eating-local | Bord Bia Origin Green: origingreen.ie | EPA Ireland water quality: epa.ie | National Biodiversity Week: biodiversityweek.ie

challenges.intro_fact: Today is World Bee Day — and it falls right in the middle of National Biodiversity Week. Ireland has around 100 species of wild bee — including 20 species of bumblebee and 77 species of solitary bee. One third of Ireland's wild bee species are threatened with extinction, including the great yellow bumblebee, now confined to a few coastal areas of the west of Ireland. Without bees, around a third of the food we eat simply would not exist.

questions.text: How much of the world's food supply depends on pollination by bees and other insects?
questions.fact: Around 35% of global food production depends on pollinators — including most fruits, vegetables, nuts and seeds. In Ireland, crops like strawberries, apples and oilseed rape depend heavily on bee pollination.

questions.text: How many of Ireland's wild bee species are currently threatened with extinction?
questions.fact: One third of Ireland's wild bee species are threatened with extinction. The great yellow bumblebee has lost over 80% of its former range and is now mainly found along the Atlantic coast of Connacht — a dramatic decline within living memory.

questions.text: The All-Ireland Pollinator Plan was launched in 2015. How many organisations had signed up as partners by 2024?
questions.fact: The All-Ireland Pollinator Plan is one of the most successful biodiversity initiatives in Irish history. Over 1,500 organisations — including local councils, farms, businesses, schools and community groups — have signed up to take actions for pollinators.

challenges.action_intro: Bees respond quickly when habitats improve — which means the actions we take in our gardens, parks and roadsides genuinely make a difference. You do not need much space to make a real impact.

actions.title: Plant one bee-friendly plant this week
actions.desc: Lavender, borage, phacelia or any native wildflower — all available in Irish garden centres from May. A single lavender plant in flower can attract dozens of bee species. Even a small pot on a windowsill counts.

actions.title: Stop cutting one patch of grass for the rest of May
actions.desc: Let whatever grows there flower. Dandelions, clover and daisies are among the most important food sources for bees — and they grow themselves. No effort, big impact.
actions.carbon: Provides immediate food source for wild bees

actions.title: Sign your organisation or community group up to the All-Ireland Pollinator Plan
actions.desc: It is free and takes 10 minutes at pollinators.ie. Every signed-up organisation commits to at least one action for pollinators — from changing mowing schedules to planting wildflowers.

challenges.resources: All-Ireland Pollinator Plan: pollinators.ie | World Bee Day — FAO: fao.org/world-bee-day | National Biodiversity Week: biodiversityweek.ie | What to plant for bees in Ireland: pollinators.ie/gardens

challenges.intro_fact: It is National Biodiversity Week. Today we connect two kinds of diversity — cultural and biological. 75% of the world's food now comes from just 12 plants and 5 animal species. This narrowing of our diet is directly linked to the narrowing of nature — as diverse wild habitats are replaced by monoculture farms growing the same crops at scale.

questions.text: How many plant species have humans used for food throughout history?
questions.fact: Humans have used around 7,000 plant species for food throughout history. Today, most of us eat fewer than 20 regularly. This loss of dietary diversity mirrors the loss of crop diversity in our fields — and makes our food system more fragile.

questions.text: Which traditional Irish crop, once a staple food, is being revived for biodiversity and food security reasons?
questions.fact: The Irish Lumper was the dominant potato variety before the Famine. It was almost lost entirely but has been revived by growers in Antrim and by the Irish Seed Savers Association. Reviving heritage varieties protects the genetic diversity in our food system.

questions.text: What is 'agrobiodiversity' and why does it matter for climate resilience?
options: Farming that uses no artificial inputs
The variety of plants, animals and microorganisms used in food and farming — which makes food systems more resilient to climate shocks
A European policy requiring crop rotation on all farms
The study of how climate change affects crop yields
questions.fact: Agrobiodiversity — diversity within and between species used in agriculture — makes food systems resilient. When a disease or climate shock hits, diverse systems recover. Monocultures do not. Ireland's seed saving movement is a direct response to this risk.

challenges.action_intro: Eating a wider variety of plants is one of the simplest ways to support biodiversity — it drives demand for diverse crops and reduces pressure on the handful of species that dominate global agriculture.

actions.title: Cook one meal this week using a vegetable or grain you have never tried before
actions.desc: Try pearl barley, spelt, or a heritage vegetable from a local market or farm shop. Eating more variety directly supports demand for agricultural biodiversity.

actions.title: Visit the Irish Seed Savers Association online
actions.desc: Visit irishseedsavers.ie — you can order heritage Irish seeds by post and grow them at home. Every garden growing heritage varieties helps preserve Ireland's food biodiversity.
actions.carbon: Preserves genetic diversity in Irish food crops

challenges.resources: Irish Seed Savers Association: irishseedsavers.ie | FAO on food biodiversity: fao.org/biodiversity | National Biodiversity Week: biodiversityweek.ie | Slow Food Ireland: slowfoodireland.com

challenges.intro_fact: Today is the UN International Day for Biological Diversity — and the final day of National Biodiversity Week in Ireland. Ireland ranks among the lowest in Europe for biodiversity health — with habitats in poor condition, species in decline and water quality under pressure. But there are also real success stories, and the direction of travel is starting to change.

questions.text: Which large wild animal has successfully returned to breed in Ireland after an absence of hundreds of years?
questions.fact: White-tailed eagles were extinct in Ireland for over 100 years before a reintroduction programme began in 2007. They now breed successfully in several counties including Kerry, Clare and Galway. It is one of Ireland's great rewilding success stories.

questions.text: What percentage of Ireland's protected habitats are currently in favourable conservation status?
questions.fact: Less than 15% of Ireland's protected habitats are in favourable condition — one of the worst records in the EU. Blanket bog, sand dunes and raised bog are among the most damaged. Significant restoration investment is now underway.

questions.text: The EU Nature Restoration Law, passed in 2024, requires member states to restore what proportion of degraded ecosystems by 2030?
questions.fact: The EU Nature Restoration Law requires member states to restore at least 20% of degraded land and sea ecosystems by 2030, rising to 90% by 2050. For Ireland this means restoring bogs, rivers, grasslands and coastal habitats at scale.

challenges.action_intro: Ireland's nature is under pressure — but it is not too late. The white-tailed eagle shows what is possible when we give nature a chance. What we do in our gardens, communities and at the ballot box all matters.

actions.title: Share one thing you learned this week about Irish biodiversity with someone
actions.desc: A friend, a colleague, or a post on social media. Talking about biodiversity is one of the most effective ways to build the social momentum for change. Most people care — they just do not know the facts.
actions.carbon: Social multiplier effect — builds climate conversation culture

actions.title: Contact your local council and ask what they are doing for the All-Ireland Pollinator Plan
actions.desc: Every council in Ireland has signed up to the Pollinator Plan. Ask what actions they are taking in your area — changing mowing schedules, planting wildflowers, or creating pollinator corridors. Your question matters.
actions.carbon: Local action is where biodiversity policy becomes real

challenges.resources: National Parks and Wildlife Service: npws.ie | EU Nature Restoration Law: ec.europa.eu/environment/nature/restoration | All-Ireland Pollinator Plan: pollinators.ie | National Biodiversity Data Centre: biodiversityireland.ie | Rewilding Europe — Ireland: rewildingeurope.com

challenges.intro_fact: Africa Day is celebrated across Ireland every year — Dublin's festival is one of the biggest outside Africa itself. Africa contributes less than 4% of global greenhouse gas emissions — yet it is the continent most affected by climate change. Droughts, floods, crop failures and displacement are already happening at scale. Climate justice asks a simple question: is it fair that those who did least to cause the problem suffer the most?

questions.text: What percentage of global greenhouse gas emissions does the entire African continent produce?
questions.fact: Africa as a whole produces less than 4% of global greenhouse gas emissions — yet is home to 17% of the world's population and faces some of the most severe climate impacts. Ireland produces more emissions per person than the average African country.

questions.text: How many people in Africa are estimated to be at risk of climate-related displacement by 2050?
questions.fact: The World Bank estimates over 200 million people in Sub-Saharan Africa could be forced to move within their own countries by 2050 due to climate impacts including drought, flooding and crop failure.

questions.text: What did Ireland pledge at COP26 in terms of international climate finance?
options: €50 million per year for climate adaptation in developing countries
€225 million per year by 2025 for climate action in developing countries
To match every euro of overseas aid with a euro of climate finance
questions.fact: At COP26, Ireland committed to providing €225 million per year in international climate finance by 2025 — one of the more ambitious pledges relative to the size of the Irish economy. The focus is on adaptation in the most vulnerable countries.

challenges.action_intro: Climate justice is not an abstract concept — it is about real people in real places facing consequences they did nothing to cause. Ireland's response — through aid, policy and individual choices — matters.

actions.title: Attend or follow Africa Day events in Dublin or your local area
actions.desc: Many Africa Day events include climate and environment themes. Check africaday.ie for events near you this weekend. Understanding the human face of climate change is the first step to caring about it.

actions.title: Choose Fairtrade or direct trade coffee, tea or chocolate this week
actions.desc: Check where your daily coffee comes from. Fairtrade and direct trade products support farmers on the frontline of climate change — and are widely available in Irish supermarkets and cafés.
actions.carbon: Supports climate-resilient farming in vulnerable regions

challenges.resources: Africa Day Ireland: africaday.ie | Our World in Data — emissions by country: ourworldindata.org/co2-emissions | World Bank Groundswell Report: worldbank.org | Trócaire climate justice: trocaire.org | Irish Aid climate finance: irishaid.ie

challenges.intro_fact: Ireland is one of the last strongholds for the Eurasian otter in Europe.
