Ireland has one of the densest otter populations in Europe — found on almost every river, lake and stretch of coastline in the country. But otters are what ecologists call an indicator species — their presence tells us a river is healthy. Where otters disappear, something has gone wrong with the water.

questions.text: Why is the otter considered an indicator species for river health?
options: They are very sensitive to water pollution and need clean, fish-rich rivers to survive
Their fur absorbs toxins making them easy to test
They build dams that filter water naturally
questions.fact: Otters sit at the top of the freshwater food chain. They need clean water, abundant fish and undisturbed riverbanks to breed. Their presence is one of the best signs that a river ecosystem is functioning well.

questions.text: What is the main threat to water quality in Irish rivers today?
options: Agricultural nutrient runoff — nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilisers and slurry
questions.fact: Only 53% of Irish water bodies are in good ecological status — and agricultural runoff is the leading cause of the rest failing. Excess nutrients cause algal blooms that strip oxygen from water, killing fish and invertebrates.

questions.text: Ireland's Water Framework Directive requires all water bodies to reach good ecological status. What is the current deadline for achieving this?
questions.fact: Under the EU Water Framework Directive, Ireland must bring all water bodies to good ecological status by 2027. Given that only 53% currently meet this standard, this is extremely challenging — and likely to be missed without significant changes in farming practice.

challenges.action_intro: Ireland's rivers and lakes are a public asset — and they are under real pressure. What each of us does at home, in the garden and in the kitchen reaches our local waterways faster than most people realise.

actions.title: Next time you are near a river or lake, stop and watch for a few minutes
actions.desc: Otters are most active at dawn and dusk — and are more common than most people realise, even in urban rivers. Knowing what lives in your local waterway is the first step to caring about it.

actions.title: Never pour cooking oil, medicines or cleaning products down the drain
actions.desc: They travel directly into waterways and affect everything living there. Cooking oil can be left to cool and disposed of in the bin. Medicines can be returned to any pharmacy in Ireland.
actions.carbon: Prevents direct pollution of local waterways

challenges.resources: National Parks and Wildlife Service — otter: npws.ie | EPA Ireland water quality: epa.ie | Inland Fisheries Ireland: fisheriesireland.ie | Clean Coasts Ireland: cleancoasts.org

challenges.intro_fact: You might not expect it — but leatherback sea turtles regularly visit Irish waters every summer, travelling from the Caribbean to feed on jellyfish off the west coast of Ireland. They are the largest reptile on earth and have existed for over 100 million years. Today they face plastic pollution, fishing bycatch and warming oceans. What happens in Irish waters matters for species that travel the entire Atlantic.

questions.text: Why do leatherback turtles come to Irish waters in summer?
options: To breed and lay eggs on Irish beaches
To feed on jellyfish which are abundant in Irish coastal waters
To follow warm currents from the Gulf Stream
questions.fact: Leatherback turtles travel thousands of kilometres from nesting beaches in the Caribbean and West Africa to feed on jellyfish in the rich waters off Ireland's west coast. Ireland's cool, jellyfish-rich seas make it a key summer feeding ground.

questions.text: How much plastic enters the world's oceans every year?
questions.fact: Around 8 million tonnes of plastic enters the ocean every year — equivalent to a rubbish truck emptying into the sea every minute. Turtles mistake plastic bags for jellyfish, ingesting them and often dying as a result.

questions.text: What percentage of leatherback sea turtles examined in studies have been found to have plastic in their digestive systems?
questions.fact: Studies consistently find plastic in over 70% of examined leatherback turtles. Plastic bags look almost identical to jellyfish underwater — turtles cannot distinguish between them. Even small amounts block digestion and can cause death.

challenges.action_intro: Most ocean plastic starts as litter on land — carried by rain and rivers to the sea. Every piece of plastic we stop from entering a drain or waterway is one less threat to the animals that depend on our ocean.

actions.title: Do a 10-minute litter pick on your nearest beach, riverbank or canal path
actions.desc: Bring a bag and pick up what you find. Clean Coasts Ireland runs regular organised beach cleans — find one near you at cleancoasts.org. They provide bags and gloves.
actions.carbon: Direct environmental impact — prevents marine pollution

actions.title: Switch from plastic bags to reusable bags permanently if you have not already
actions.desc: Check your freezer bags, sandwich bags and cling film too — all have reusable or compostable alternatives now available in Irish supermarkets. Single-use plastic bags are among the most common items in Irish marine surveys.
actions.carbon: Reduces one of the most harmful forms of marine plastic

challenges.resources: Irish Whale and Dolphin Group: iwdg.ie | Clean Coasts Ireland: cleancoasts.org | UNEP ocean plastics: unep.org/explore-topics/oceans-seas | Plastic Free July — start preparing: plasticfreejuly.org

challenges.intro_fact: Amnesty International was founded on the principle that human rights are universal. Climate change is now recognised as a human rights issue — by the UN, by the courts, and increasingly by governments. In 2021, an Irish Supreme Court ruling found that the government's climate action plan was not specific enough to meet Ireland's own legal obligations. Citizens took the state to court — and won.

questions.text: In what year did the United Nations officially recognise a clean, healthy and sustainable environment as a universal human right?
questions.fact: In July 2022, the UN General Assembly passed a resolution recognising access to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment as a universal human right. This has significant implications for climate litigation and accountability worldwide.

questions.text: Which Irish climate case resulted in the Supreme Court ruling against the government's climate action plan in 2021?
options: Friends of the Irish Environment v An Bord Pleanála
Friends of the Irish Environment v The Government of Ireland
Greenpeace Ireland v Department of Environment
Climate Case Ireland v An Taoiseach
questions.fact: In July 2021 the Irish Supreme Court ruled that the government's National Mitigation Plan was too vague to be legally compliant with Ireland's own Climate Action and Low Carbon Development Act — a landmark ruling and one of the first successful national climate cases in Europe.

questions.text: Which country was the subject of the first successful human rights climate case at the European Court of Human Rights, ruled in 2024?
questions.fact: In April 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled in favour of a group of Swiss women — KlimaSeniorinnen — finding that Switzerland violated their human rights by failing to act sufficiently on climate change. The first successful climate human rights case at European court level.

challenges.action_intro: Climate accountability is a civic act, not just a legal one. The Irish Supreme Court case shows that when citizens organise and push, governments must respond. You do not need to be a lawyer to play a part.

actions.title: Read about the Irish Supreme Court climate case
actions.desc: Visit friendsoftheirishenvironment.org — it shows what citizens can achieve when they hold governments accountable. Understanding the case takes about 5 minutes and changes how you see climate policy.

actions.title: Write to or email your local TD about one specific climate or nature issue
actions.desc: You do not need to be an expert — just a constituent. Find your TD at oireachtas.ie and write one short, specific, polite message about something you care about. TDs respond to constituent contact.

challenges.resources: Friends of the Irish Environment: friendsoftheirishenvironment.org | Amnesty International Ireland: amnesty.ie | Climate Rights International: climaterights.org | Contact your TD: oireachtas.ie

challenges.intro_fact: Ireland has a proud tradition of UN peacekeeping — with Irish troops serving in conflicts around the world since 1958. There is a growing body of evidence that climate change is a threat multiplier — it does not start wars, but it makes existing tensions worse. Droughts reduce food and water, displacement increases, and competition over shrinking resources fuels conflict. The Irish Defence Forces are already factoring climate into their planning.

questions.text: What does the term 'climate threat multiplier' mean?
options: Climate change makes existing social, economic and political tensions worse, increasing the risk of conflict
Military activity is a major contributor to climate change
Climate refugees always move to conflict zones
questions.fact: Climate change does not cause conflict directly — but drought, food insecurity and displacement all make fragile situations more dangerous. The Pentagon, NATO and the EU all formally recognise climate as a security risk.

questions.text: What percentage of global military emissions are produced by the United States armed forces alone?
questions.fact: The US military is the single largest institutional consumer of fossil fuels in the world, responsible for over 50% of global military greenhouse gas emissions. Military emissions are largely excluded from national climate targets under current international agreements.

questions.text: Ireland's first National Risk Assessment to formally include climate change as a national security threat was published in which year?
questions.fact: Ireland's 2023 National Risk Assessment formally identified climate change as a top-tier national security risk for the first time — alongside cybersecurity and geopolitical instability. The Irish Defence Forces now consider climate impacts in operational planning.

challenges.action_intro: Connecting the dots between climate change and global security is one of the most important shifts in understanding. Ireland's peacekeeping tradition gives us a particular responsibility to support climate stability worldwide.

actions.title: Read Trócaire's annual report on climate and conflict
actions.desc: Visit trocaire.org — it shows the real human stories behind the data on climate displacement and conflict. Ireland's overseas aid work is directly connected to climate resilience in the most vulnerable regions.
actions.carbon: Builds understanding of climate justice and global impact

actions.title: Next time you see a conflict or displacement story in the news, look up whether climate is a contributing factor
actions.desc: Use reliefweb.int or ceobs.org to find the environmental context behind global crises. It usually is a factor — and knowing that changes how you understand the news.
actions.carbon: Awareness — connecting climate to global events

challenges.resources: Trócaire climate and conflict: trocaire.org | Conflict and Environment Observatory: ceobs.org | IPCC Sixth Assessment Report: ipcc.ch | Irish Defence Forces: military.ie

challenges.intro_fact: June is a big month for our planet. EU Sustainable Energy Week runs all month. Today is World Reef Day, a good moment to think about what our ocean is telling us. Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor but support about 25% of all marine species. Ireland has no tropical coral reefs, but it does have cold-water coral ecosystems off its Atlantic coast, some of the largest in Europe. These deep-sea reefs are threatened by warming water and ocean acidification caused by rising CO2 in the atmosphere.

questions.text: What percentage of all marine species depend on coral reefs for habitat?
questions.fact: Cold-water and tropical coral reefs together support roughly a quarter of all ocean species despite covering a tiny fraction of the sea floor. Ireland's cold-water corals are among the most extensive in European waters.

questions.text: Roughly how deep are Ireland's cold-water coral reefs found off the Atlantic coast?
options: They are found only in shallow coastal waters
questions.fact: Ireland's cold-water coral reefs sit at depths of roughly 200 to 1,000 metres off the western Atlantic coast and are among the most extensive in European waters. They are threatened by warming seas and ocean acidification.

questions.text: In 2024, what proportion of the world's coral reefs experienced bleaching conditions due to record sea surface temperatures?
questions.fact: In 2024, around 75% of the world's coral reefs were impacted by coral bleaching due to rising water temperatures, the most widespread bleaching event ever recorded.

challenges.action_intro: Our ocean is one of the most powerful climate regulators on Earth and it is under growing pressure. Small actions on land reach the sea faster than most people realise.

actions.title: Check the sustainability label on seafood before you buy it this week
actions.desc: Look for the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) label on fish. It is the most widely recognised standard for sustainably caught seafood and is available in most Irish supermarkets.

actions.title: Reduce one plastic item you use this week
actions.desc: Plastic pollution is one of the top threats to marine ecosystems. Refuse a plastic bag, straw, or coffee cup lid this week and replace it with a reusable alternative.
actions.carbon: Reduces plastic entering Irish waterways and the ocean

challenges.resources: Marine Institute Ireland: marine.ie | IUCN Cold Water Coral Portal: iucn.org | Clean Coasts Ireland: cleancoasts.org

challenges.intro_fact: EU Sustainable Energy Week is an annual European event that brings together people, businesses, and communities around one question: how do we power our lives without cooking the planet? Ireland's energy story is worth knowing. For most of the last century, we imported almost everything we burned. That is slowly changing, faster than many people realise.

questions.text: What share of Ireland's electricity came from renewable sources in 2024?
questions.fact: Ireland's overall renewable electricity share reached 41.3% in 2024, the highest figure to date. Solar PV generation was up 69% and heat pump output was up 19%.

questions.text: What percentage of Ireland's total energy still came from fossil fuels in 2023?
questions.fact: In 2023, 82.6% of Ireland's total energy still came from fossil fuels, highlighting how much further the transition needs to go beyond just the electricity sector.

questions.text: What is Ireland's renewable energy target for 2030 under the EU Renewable Energy Directive?
questions.fact: Ireland's 2030 target is 43% of overall energy from renewables, covering electricity, heat, and transport. In 2024 Ireland reached 13.5% of overall energy from renewables, meaning there is still a significant gap to close.

challenges.action_intro: Ireland's clean energy transition is happening but it is not fast enough. The choices consumers, businesses, and communities make all influence the pace of change.

actions.title: Check if your electricity supplier offers a green tariff
actions.desc: Many Irish energy suppliers now offer tariffs where your electricity is matched to renewable generation. Switching can take less than 10 minutes online and often costs the same or less.

actions.title: Look into the SEAI home upgrade grant scheme
actions.desc: Grants of up to EUR 1,800 for solar panels and up to EUR 12,500 for heat pumps are available in 2026. Even reading through the options at seai.ie is a useful first step.
actions.carbon: Home upgrades can cut heating emissions by up to 70%

challenges.resources: SEAI grants: seai.ie/grants | EU Sustainable Energy Week: eusew.eu | SEAI Energy in Ireland report: seai.ie

challenges.intro_fact: Today is World Bicycle Day. The United Nations created it in 2018 to recognise that the bicycle is a simple, affordable, and clean way to get around. In Ireland, getting more people cycling is a key part of the national climate plan. Transport is one of Ireland's biggest sources of emissions, and private cars dominate. But the numbers are starting to shift.

questions.text: What share of peak-hour commuters into Dublin city centre used sustainable transport in 2024?
questions.fact: In 2024, 73% of peak-hour commuters crossing into Dublin city centre used sustainable transport, including cycling, walking, and public transport, up from previous years.

questions.text: Since 2020, how much has the Irish government invested in walking and cycling infrastructure?
questions.fact: By 2024, Ireland's total active travel investment since 2020 surpassed the EUR 1 billion mark, delivering over 600km of new cycling and walking infrastructure across the country.

questions.text: Ireland's Bike to Work scheme covers the purchase of an e-bike or cargo bike up to what value?
questions.fact: Since 2022, the Bike to Work scheme covers e-bikes and cargo bikes up to EUR 3,000, with standard bikes covered up to EUR 1,500. The scheme saves up to 52% on the cost through salary sacrifice.

challenges.action_intro: Most Irish commutes are short enough to cycle but infrastructure and habit are the barriers. One change a week builds momentum faster than you think.

actions.title: Try cycling or walking for one journey this week you would usually make by car
actions.desc: Any trip under 3km is often faster by bike once you factor in parking. Give it one try this week and notice how you feel.

actions.title: Check if your employer is signed up to the Bike to Work scheme
actions.desc: Visit biketowork.ie -- it takes 5 minutes. The scheme saves you up to 52% on a new bike or e-bike through salary sacrifice.

challenges.resources: Cycling Ireland: cyclingireland.ie | IrishCycle.com | Bike to Work Scheme: revenue.ie

challenges.intro_fact: When we talk about clean energy, we usually think of electricity. But heating our homes and businesses uses even more energy in Ireland. Most Irish heating still comes from oil and gas. That is one reason why heat pumps and home insulation are so important. In 2025, heat pumps delivered more renewable energy in Ireland than all solar farms and rooftop panels combined.

questions.text: What share of Irish homes' heating currently comes from renewable sources?
questions.fact: In 2024, the renewable heat share reached 7.9% in Ireland, a new high but well below the targets set in Ireland's Climate Action Plan. Home heating is one of the biggest opportunities remaining.

questions.text: What percentage of Irish homes use oil as their primary heating source?
questions.fact: Around 40% of Irish homes use oil as their primary heating source, rising to over 60% in rural areas. Oil heating produces roughly 3x more CO2 than a modern heat pump running on Irish grid electricity.

questions.text: In 2025, what source delivered more renewable energy in Ireland than all solar farms and rooftop panels combined?
questions.fact: In 2025, heat pumps delivered more renewable energy than all solar farms and rooftop panels combined, making them the single largest source of renewable heat in Ireland. Uptake is accelerating rapidly.

challenges.action_intro: Home heating is the single biggest source of household emissions in Ireland and the biggest opportunity for change. Even small steps like draught-proofing make a real difference.

actions.title: Turn your heating thermostat down by one degree
actions.desc: Reducing your thermostat by just one degree can cut your heating costs by around 10% and reduce your home's carbon emissions noticeably over a full year.

actions.title: Look into the SEAI heat pump grant if you heat with oil
actions.desc: The SEAI grant covers up to EUR 12,500 towards switching from oil to a heat pump in 2026. Visit seai.ie/grants -- even reading the options is a useful first step.
actions.carbon: Switching from oil to heat pump saves ~2-3 tonnes CO2 per year

challenges.resources: SEAI Better Energy Homes: seai.ie/grants/home-energy-upgrades | SEAI heat pump guide: seai.ie | Tipperary Energy Agency: tea.ie

challenges.intro_fact: Today is the biggest global environmental awareness day of the year. World Environment Day 2026 theme is 'Now for Climate', calling on governments, businesses, and individuals to move urgently. In Ireland, the EPA's latest projections show that even with all planned climate policies in place, Ireland could achieve only up to 25% emissions reduction by 2030, against a legal target of 51%. The gap is wide. But every action counts.

questions.text: What is the official theme of World Environment Day 2026?
questions.fact: The theme of World Environment Day 2026 is 'Now For Climate', calling on governments, businesses, and individuals to move urgently on climate action. The event is hosted in Baku, Azerbaijan.

questions.text: Ireland has a legal target to cut emissions by 51% by 2030 compared to 2018. What does the EPA project Ireland will actually achieve if all planned measures are implemented?
questions.fact: The EPA's May 2026 projections show Ireland could achieve only up to 25% emissions reduction by 2030, well short of its 51% legal target. This gap could cost Ireland between EUR 3 billion and EUR 26 billion in emissions allowances.

questions.text: In 2025, Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions from power generation and industry covered by the EU ETS fell. By how much?
questions.fact: In 2025, Ireland's ETS-covered emissions fell by 5.5%, reflecting the shift toward cleaner energy and more sustainable manufacturing. But emissions from transport, agriculture, and heating remain the bigger challenge.

challenges.action_intro: The Earth is sending us signals. Today is a day to send one back. Every action, conversation, and vote on climate matters.

actions.title: Register your action on the UNEP global map
actions.desc: Visit worldenvironmentday.global -- it takes two minutes to register a pledge and join a global movement of people acting on climate.

actions.title: Share one climate fact with someone today using #NowForClimate
actions.desc: Pick the most surprising thing you learned from today's challenge and share it with one person, in conversation or on social media. Breaking the spiral of silence on climate is one of the most powerful things you can do.

challenges.resources: World Environment Day 2026: worldenvironmentday.global | EPA Ireland emissions data: epa.ie/ghg | Climate Action Plan Ireland: gov.ie/climateaction

challenges.intro_fact: Today is World Oceans Day, and this week is the start of Great Big Green Week in Ireland. Ireland has one of the largest sea areas in Europe relative to its land size. Our ocean absorbs around 30% of the CO2 we release and produces about 50% of the world's oxygen. Yet we are filling it with plastic. As of 2025, an estimated 75 to 199 million tonnes of plastic waste is already in the world's oceans.

questions.text: Roughly what percentage of marine litter is made up of plastic?
questions.fact: Plastic accounts for approximately 85% of all marine litter globally, and volumes entering the ocean are expected to nearly triple by 2040 without significant policy and behaviour change.

questions.text: What percentage of protected marine environments around Ireland's coastline were found to contain microplastics?
questions.fact: A study found microplastics in 90% of protected Irish marine environments, with researchers noting the problem affects every part of the coastline, from Kerry to Donegal.

questions.text: Ireland launched a Deposit Return Scheme in February 2024. What measurable impact did it have on marine litter by the end of 2024?
options: No impact was recorded in the first year
Bottle and can litter on Irish shores fell to the lowest average in 25 years
Marine litter increased because other types replaced bottles and cans
It reduced marine litter by 10% overall
questions.fact: The Coastwatch Annual Marine Litter Survey found that 2024 recorded the lowest average levels of bottle and can litter on Irish shores in 25 years, a direct result of the Deposit Return Scheme.

challenges.action_intro: What we do on land ends up in the sea. Great Big Green Week is a perfect moment to connect local community action to the health of our ocean.

actions.title: Find a Great Big Green Week event near you
actions.desc: Visit greatbiggreenweek.com to find a local event this week -- from beach cleans to sustainability talks. Community action on climate and nature is happening all around Ireland right now.

actions.title: Use the Re-Turn app to return your bottles and cans this week
actions.desc: Find your nearest return point and bring your plastic bottles and aluminium cans. You get your deposit back, and the materials stay in the circular economy and out of the ocean.

challenges.resources: Great Big Green Week Ireland: greatbiggreenweek.com | Clean Coasts Ireland: cleancoasts.org | Re-Turn Ireland: re-turn.ie

challenges.intro_fact: This week is Men's Health Week across Ireland and the UK. Men are statistically less likely to talk about mental health or seek help. Research consistently shows that time in nature reduces stress, anxiety, and low mood. Combining green spaces and community connection is one of the most effective and underused wellbeing tools we have.

questions.text: Studies show that a 20-minute walk in a green space can reduce cortisol levels by approximately how much?
questions.fact: Research published in Frontiers in Psychology found that urban nature walks of around 20 minutes can reduce cortisol levels by approximately 21%, with measurable effects on mood and stress.

questions.text: What does the term 'green prescribing' refer to?
options: Doctors recommending time in nature as part of healthcare
Using plant-based medicines instead of pharmaceuticals
questions.fact: Green prescribing involves health professionals recommending activities in natural environments -- such as walking groups, gardening, or outdoor exercise -- as part of care for mental and physical health conditions. It is growing across Irish primary care.

questions.text: According to the WHO, physical inactivity is one of the leading risk factors for what?
options: Non-communicable diseases including heart disease, diabetes, and some cancers
questions.fact: The WHO identifies physical inactivity as one of the leading risk factors for non-communicable diseases globally, contributing to conditions such as heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and certain cancers.

challenges.action_intro: Looking after nature and looking after yourself are the same thing. Men's Health Week is a good prompt to make time for both.

actions.title: Suggest a walk or outdoor lunch to a male colleague, friend, or family member this week
actions.desc: You do not need to make it about mental health -- just the walk. Getting outside together is one of the simplest and most effective things two people can do for each other.
actions.carbon: Zero carbon and significant wellbeing benefit

actions.title: Visit a green space near you that you have never been to before
actions.desc: Most Irish towns and cities have parks, canal walks, or nature areas within easy reach. Find one you have never visited and go this week.

challenges.resources: Men's Health Week Ireland: menshealthweek.ie | HSE Social Prescribing: hse.ie | Samaritans Ireland: samaritans.org (116 123)

challenges.intro_fact: Great Big Green Week is a national celebration of community-led climate and nature action happening across Ireland this week. Community action matters because it creates visible change that inspires others. It also builds the kind of local knowledge and networks that make longer-term change possible. Ireland has proven this more than once.

questions.text: Ireland's plastic bag levy in 2002 was a world first. By how much did plastic bag use fall in the first year?
questions.fact: Within the first months of Ireland's plastic bag levy introduction, consumption fell by around 90%, removing over a billion bags from circulation per year. Ireland was the first country in the world to introduce this policy.

questions.text: In which year was Ireland's first Climate Action Plan legally required under the Climate Action and Low Carbon Development (Amendment) Act?
questions.fact: The Climate Action and Low Carbon Development (Amendment) Act 2021 made it a legal requirement for Ireland to adopt Climate Action Plans with binding carbon budgets, one of the strongest climate frameworks in Europe.

questions.text: Research shows that social norms can shift when what proportion of a community commits to a new behaviour?
questions.fact: Research backed by the IPCC shows that just 10 to 25% of committed individuals can shift a social norm for the whole group. You do not need everyone -- just enough people willing to act visibly.

challenges.action_intro: Community action is not a soft option. It is one of the most effective levers for change we have. Find something happening near you this week.

actions.title: Find a Great Big Green Week event and sign up
actions.desc: Visit greatbiggreenweek.com -- events range from beach cleans to sustainability workshops and community tree planting. Most are free.

actions.title: Contact your local authority and ask what community climate support is available
actions.desc: Most local councils in Ireland now have a climate action officer and community grants. A simple email or phone call can open up support you did not know existed.

challenges.resources: Great Big Green Week: greatbiggreenweek.com | Stop Climate Chaos Ireland: stopclimatechaos.ie | An Taisce Green Schools: greenschoolsireland.org

challenges.intro_fact: Men's Health Week continues. Ireland has some of the most stunning natural landscapes in Europe, yet research shows Irish people spend up to 90% of their time indoors. The irony is that what we are fighting to protect through climate action -- clean air, green spaces, access to nature -- is also what helps us feel better and live longer.

questions.text: Ireland has six national parks. Which is the largest by area?
questions.fact: Ballycroy National Park in Mayo is Ireland's largest national park by area, covering approximately 11,000 hectares of blanket bog and Atlantic mountain terrain. All six national parks are free to enter.

questions.text: Killarney National Park holds a special distinction for forest cover. What is it?
options: It is Ireland's most visited park
It contains the most extensive cover of native forest remaining in Ireland
It is the only national park with a UNESCO World Heritage designation
It has the highest number of mammal species of any Irish park
questions.fact: Killarney National Park contains the most extensive covering of native forest remaining in Ireland and was designated a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve in 1981. It is also home to Ireland's only wild herd of native red deer.

questions.text: How much time in nature per week is linked to significantly better health and wellbeing, according to a major UK study?
questions.fact: Spending at least 2 hours per week in nature is linked to significantly better health and wellbeing -- even in short visits spread across the week. The effect holds for people of all ages and fitness levels.

challenges.action_intro: Ireland's national parks are free, extraordinary, and mostly empty. Plan a visit this summer -- it is good for you and it connects you to what we are working to protect.

actions.title: Plan a visit to one of Ireland's six national parks this summer
actions.desc: Killarney, Glenveagh, Connemara, Ballycroy, Wicklow Mountains, and the Burren. All are free to enter. Pick the one closest to you and put a date in the diary.
actions.carbon: Zero carbon and significant wellbeing benefit

actions.title: Look up social prescribing services in your local area through the HSE
actions.desc: If you or someone you know is struggling with stress or low mood, nature-based activities are increasingly available through GPs and community health networks. Ask about it.
actions.carbon: Nature access is a public health issue

challenges.resources: National Parks and Wildlife Service: npws.ie | HSE Social Prescribing: hse.ie | Leave No Trace Ireland: leavenotraceireland.org

challenges.intro_fact: Today is the last day of Great Big Green Week 2026. Ireland's plastic bag levy is one of the most powerful examples of collective action in environmental history. Within months of a 15 cent charge being introduced in 2002, over a billion plastic bags disappeared from circulation. That mindset -- small shifts creating big outcomes -- is exactly what climate action needs at scale.

questions.text: Before Ireland's plastic bag levy, how many bags were given out free in Irish shops every year?
questions.fact: Prior to the levy, over 1.2 billion plastic bags were dispensed free at Irish retail outlets annually, equivalent to roughly 328 bags per person per year. Within months of the levy, that number collapsed.

questions.text: Revenue from Ireland's plastic bag levy is ring-fenced for what purpose?
options: It goes directly to the national budget
It is given to retailers to cover costs
An Environment Fund supporting anti-litter, EPA research, and community projects
It subsidises the cost of reusable bags
questions.fact: Revenue from the plastic bag levy is ring-fenced for an Environment Fund that supports anti-litter initiatives, EPA research and development, and community environmental projects. Over EUR 196 million has been collected since 2002.

questions.text: By 2025, bottle and can litter in Irish towns had fallen by approximately how much following the Deposit Return Scheme?
questions.fact: By 2025, plastic bottles and cans were 60% less common as litter in Irish towns and cities, compared to before the Deposit Return Scheme was introduced in February 2024.

challenges.action_intro: Policy works when people demand it. And behaviour change works when communities support it. Ireland has proven both. The next chapter is being written now.

actions.title: Share one thing you did or learned during Great Big Green Week
actions.desc: Tell a friend, post on social media, or bring it up at work. Talking openly about what you are doing on sustainability is one of the most effective ways to normalise it for others.

actions.title: Sign up to the Clean Coasts network
actions.desc: Clean Coasts Ireland connects thousands of volunteers around Ireland's coastline. Signing up takes two minutes and keeps you connected to marine action all year round.

challenges.resources: Great Big Green Week: greatbiggreenweek.com | Clean Coasts: cleancoasts.org | Stop Climate Chaos Ireland: stopclimatechaos.ie

challenges.intro_fact: For a country known for its rain, Ireland has been surprisingly slow to embrace solar energy. But that is changing fast. Solar panels work on daylight, not direct sunshine, which means they generate electricity year-round in Irish conditions. In 2024, solar PV generation was up 69%. By 2026, more than 170,000 Irish homes had rooftop solar installed.

questions.text: How many Irish homes had rooftop solar panels installed by 2026?
questions.fact: By 2026, more than 170,000 Irish homes had rooftop solar panels installed, and Ireland added over 1 GW of solar capacity in 2025 alone. During summer months solar supplied more than one-fifth of national electricity demand.

questions.text: A typical 4 kWp rooftop solar system in Ireland can generate approximately what proportion of a household's annual electricity needs?
questions.fact: A typical 4 kWp rooftop system generates around 40% of an average Irish household's annual electricity needs, with summer generation significantly higher and winter lower.

questions.text: What SEAI grant is available in 2026 for homeowners installing solar PV panels?
questions.fact: In 2026, SEAI offers a grant of up to EUR 1,800 for residential solar PV installations, along with 0% VAT on supply and installation. Homeowners can also earn microgeneration export payments for surplus electricity.

challenges.action_intro: Your roof could be generating clean electricity right now. The grants, the technology, and the export payments are all in place. It is worth a conversation.

actions.title: Use the SEAI solar calculator to estimate savings at your address
actions.desc: The free calculator at seai.ie estimates generation, savings, and payback time for any Irish address. It takes about five minutes.

actions.title: Get a free solar assessment from a registered SEAI installer
actions.desc: A registered SEAI installer can assess your roof and give you a no-obligation quote. The SEAI website lists approved contractors by county.
actions.carbon: Average solar system saves ~1 tonne CO2 per year

challenges.resources: SEAI Solar Grants: seai.ie/grants/solar-electricity | Community Power: communitypower.ie | Electric Ireland Microgeneration: electricireland.ie

challenges.intro_fact: Today is World Sea Turtle Day. Sea turtles have been on Earth for over 100 million years. Today all seven species are either vulnerable, endangered, or critically endangered. Leatherback sea turtles regularly appear off the Irish coast, travelling thousands of kilometres from tropical nesting beaches in the Caribbean to feed on jellyfish in Irish waters. Plastic bags look almost identical to jellyfish underwater.

questions.text: What percentage of baby sea turtles have been found to have plastic in their stomachs?
questions.fact: Studies have found that 100% of baby sea turtles examined have plastic in their stomachs, reflecting the scale of plastic pollution across the ocean environments where they hatch and feed.

questions.text: Which sea turtle species is most commonly reported off the Irish coastline?
questions.fact: Leatherback sea turtles are the species most commonly reported off Irish waters. They travel vast distances from the Caribbean and West Africa, following jellyfish populations into the North Atlantic each summer.

questions.text: What proportion of all plastic ever produced has been recycled globally?
questions.fact: Only around 9% of all plastics ever produced have been recycled globally. The remainder is still in use, in landfill, or has been released into the environment including the ocean.

challenges.action_intro: Most ocean plastic starts as litter on land, carried by rain and rivers to the sea. Every piece we stop from entering a drain or waterway is one less threat to the animals that depend on our ocean.

actions.title: Refuse a plastic straw or lid the next time you buy a drink
actions.desc: Most cafes and takeaways will happily skip the straw or plastic lid if you ask. It takes one second and removes one piece of plastic from circulation.

actions.title: Report any sea turtle sighting off the Irish coast
actions.desc: If you spot a sea turtle off the Irish coast, report it to the Irish Whale and Dolphin Group at iwdg.ie. Every sighting contributes to national marine monitoring.
actions.carbon: Supports citizen science and marine conservation

challenges.resources: Irish Whale and Dolphin Group: iwdg.ie | Clean Coasts Ireland: cleancoasts.org | Sea Turtle Conservancy: conserveturtles.org

challenges.intro_fact: Today the UN marks World Day to Combat Desertification and Drought. Ireland may not be a desert, but our soils are under pressure. Irish peatlands store approximately 4 billion tonnes of carbon, more than all Irish forests combined. When bogs are drained for farming or cut for fuel, they release that carbon. Ireland is one of the largest emitters of peatland-related carbon in Europe relative to its size.

questions.text: What is a peatland or bog?
options: A type of coastal wetland formed by seawater
A waterlogged landscape where plant matter accumulates slowly over thousands of years, storing large amounts of carbon
A naturally occurring desert habitat found in the midlands
A low-lying area prone to flooding after rain
questions.fact: Peatlands are waterlogged ecosystems where organic matter, mainly from sphagnum moss, accumulates over millennia. They are among the most carbon-dense ecosystems on Earth and take thousands of years to form.

questions.text: Approximately how much carbon is stored in Irish peatlands?
questions.fact: Irish peatlands are estimated to store approximately 4 billion tonnes of carbon, making them one of the most significant natural carbon stores in the country. Protecting them is one of Ireland's most important nature-based climate actions.

questions.text: What does the EU Nature Restoration Law, agreed in 2024, require member states to do by 2030?
options: Have restoration measures in place for at least 20% of degraded land and sea areas
Protect 30% of all land as national parks
Plant 1 billion trees across the EU
questions.fact: The EU Nature Restoration Law requires member states to restore at least 20% of their degraded land and sea areas by 2030, rising to all degraded ecosystems by 2050. For Ireland this means restoring bogs, rivers, grasslands, and coastal habitats at scale.

challenges.action_intro: Protecting and restoring Irish peatlands is one of the highest-impact climate and biodiversity actions available. It starts with understanding what these landscapes are and why they matter.

actions.title: Switch to peat-free compost this year
actions.desc: Peat-free compost is now widely available in Irish garden centres and supermarkets. It performs just as well and avoids contributing to peatland destruction.

actions.title: Support the Irish Peatland Conservation Council
actions.desc: Visit ipcc.ie to learn about bog restoration in Ireland and how to get involved. You can adopt a bog, join a guided walk, or donate to restoration work.
actions.carbon: Peatland restoration stores and sequesters carbon

challenges.resources: Irish Peatland Conservation Council: ipcc.ie | NPWS habitat restoration: npws.ie | EU Nature Restoration Law: environment.ec.europa.eu

challenges.intro_fact: Ireland is one of the windiest countries in Europe. This is not always celebrated, but it should be. Our wind resource is an enormous competitive advantage in the energy transition. Ireland already has over 300 wind farms and more than 5,000 MW of installed onshore capacity. The next frontier is offshore wind, which could power not just Ireland but export electricity across Europe.

questions.text: What share of Ireland's electricity came from wind power in 2023?
questions.fact: Just over a third, or 33.7%, of Ireland's electricity came from wind in 2023, making it the single largest source of electricity generation. On high-wind days in 2025, wholesale electricity prices were almost half those on low-wind days.

questions.text: What is Ireland's target for installed offshore wind capacity by 2030?
questions.fact: Ireland's Climate Action Plan sets a 2030 target of 5 GW of installed offshore wind capacity, alongside 9 GW of onshore wind. Ireland's offshore wind resource has been estimated at more than 10 times its current total electricity demand.

questions.text: On high-wind days in Ireland in 2025, how did wholesale electricity prices compare to fossil-fuel-heavy days?
options: They were almost half the price
questions.fact: In 2025, the average wholesale electricity price on high-wind days was around EUR 76 per MWh, compared to nearly EUR 149 on low-wind, fossil-fuel-heavy days -- almost double. Clean energy is cheaper energy.

challenges.action_intro: Wind is Ireland's natural competitive advantage in the energy transition. The faster we build it, the lower our energy costs and emissions.

actions.title: Check if your electricity supplier is sourcing wind power
actions.desc: Look for a green tariff if your current supplier is not using renewable sources. Switching takes about 10 minutes and supports demand for wind energy.

actions.title: Write to your local TD about offshore wind planning in your area
actions.desc: Offshore wind projects are being delayed by planning and grid connection issues. A short, polite message to your TD asking about local progress takes five minutes and makes a difference.

challenges.resources: Wind Energy Ireland: windenergyireland.com | EirGrid (grid operator): eirgrid.ie | SEAI Wind Energy: seai.ie/technologies/wind-energy

challenges.intro_fact: Summer means barbecues, picnics, and more food bought than is often needed. Ireland wastes around 1 million tonnes of food every year, most of it in our homes. When food ends up in landfill, it produces methane -- a greenhouse gas around 80 times more powerful than CO2 over a 20-year period. Reducing food waste is one of the top five climate actions globally.

questions.text: Where does most food waste in Ireland come from?
questions.fact: The majority of food waste in Ireland originates in households, making consumer behaviour one of the most impactful areas for action. Irish households throw away an estimated EUR 700 worth of food every year.

questions.text: How many times more potent is methane as a greenhouse gas compared to CO2 over a 20-year period?
questions.fact: Methane is approximately 80 times more potent than CO2 as a greenhouse gas over a 20-year timeframe. Food rotting in landfill is one of the most significant sources of methane emissions in Ireland.

questions.text: According to Project Drawdown, reducing food waste ranks how among all global climate solutions?
questions.fact: Reducing food waste ranks in the top 5 climate solutions globally according to Project Drawdown -- higher than solar panels, electric vehicles, or wind power. It saves money and emissions at the same time.

challenges.action_intro: Wasting less food is one of the single highest-impact climate actions you can take -- and it saves you money. A fridge check before shopping is all it takes to start.

actions.title: Check your fridge before your next food shop and plan meals around what is already there
actions.desc: Before you go shopping this week, open your fridge and write a list based only on what you actually need. Stick to it. It takes five minutes and saves money.
actions.carbon: Could save EUR 700 and significant CO2 per year

actions.title: Freeze bread, meat, or leftovers before they go off
actions.desc: Most foods can be frozen before they spoil. Bread, meat, cheese, and cooked leftovers all freeze well. Freeze today rather than bin tomorrow.

challenges.resources: Stop Food Waste Ireland: stopfoodwaste.ie | EPA Food Waste Resources: epa.ie | Love Food Hate Waste: mywaste.ie

challenges.intro_fact: Today is World Rainforest Day. When you think of rainforests, you probably picture the Amazon. But there is a rare and ancient type of rainforest right here in Ireland. Temperate Atlantic rainforest thrives along Ireland's western seaboard, in places like Killarney, Glengarriff, and Glenveagh. It is draped in mosses, liverworts, and ferns and is one of the rarest habitats in the world. Most people in Ireland have never heard of it.

questions.text: What is the main feature that qualifies Ireland's Atlantic woodland as a rainforest?
options: It receives more than 3,000mm of rainfall per year
It has a closed canopy of tropical tree species
High rainfall, mild temperatures, and rich communities of mosses, liverworts, and ferns that grow on the trees themselves
It contains large predators like wolves that control the ecosystem
questions.fact: Ireland's temperate rainforests are defined by high rainfall, mild Atlantic temperatures, and the extraordinary richness of mosses, liverworts, and ferns that grow on the trees themselves, making them the country's richest terrestrial habitat.

questions.text: How much of Ireland was covered by this type of ancient forest before humans arrived, approximately 7,000 years ago?
questions.fact: Ancient damp-climate oceanic forest once covered an estimated 80% of Ireland before the arrival of humans around 7,000 BCE. Today only small fragments survive, mostly in national parks along the western seaboard.

questions.text: What is the main threat to Ireland's remaining temperate rainforest fragments today?
options: Rising temperatures drying out the habitat
Deer overgrazing, invasive rhododendron, and the absence of large predators
Coastal flooding due to sea level rise
questions.fact: Ireland's remaining rainforest fragments face serious threats from sika deer overgrazing and invasive rhododendron, which chokes out native woodland regeneration. The absence of large predators means deer numbers go unchecked.

challenges.action_intro: Ireland's rainforest is one of the best-kept secrets in European nature. Visiting it, sharing the story, and supporting restoration are all things you can do.

actions.title: Plan a visit to Killarney National Park or Glengarriff Woods
actions.desc: Both are free to enter and contain Ireland's finest surviving rainforest. Bring waterproofs and look for the layers of moss, lichen, and fern that cover every surface.
actions.carbon: Builds connection to Ireland's rarest habitat

actions.title: Support the Wild Atlantic Rainforest Restoration Project
actions.desc: Visit hometree.ie to learn about rainforest restoration in Ireland and how to contribute. Every native tree planted is a step toward restoring this ancient landscape.
actions.carbon: Native woodland restoration stores carbon and supports biodiversity

challenges.resources: Hometree Wild Atlantic Rainforest: hometree.ie | Irish Wildlife Trust: iwt.ie | NPWS woodland habitats: npws.ie

challenges.intro_fact: The summer solstice just passed -- the longest day of the year. June is when solar panels in Ireland work hardest. During summer months, solar supplied more than one-fifth of national electricity demand. Irish homeowners with solar panels can now earn microgeneration export payments for surplus electricity sent back to the grid.

questions.text: Solar panels in Ireland generate electricity from what?
options: UV radiation only available in summer
questions.fact: Solar panels work from daylight, not direct sunshine. They generate electricity year-round in Irish conditions, though output is highest in the long summer days of June and July.

questions.text: A typical 4 kWp rooftop solar system covers what proportion of an Irish household's annual electricity needs?
questions.fact: A typical 4 kWp rooftop system generates around 40% of an average Irish household's annual electricity needs, with a payback period of around 7 to 10 years depending on usage.

questions.text: What is the term for the payment Irish homeowners receive for surplus solar electricity exported back to the grid?
questions.fact: Irish homeowners with solar panels can earn microgeneration export payments for surplus electricity sent back to the grid. Rates vary by supplier but were around 18 to 20 cent per kWh in 2026.

challenges.action_intro: Your roof could be generating clean electricity and cutting your bills at the same time. The grants, the technology, and the export payments are all in place.

actions.title: Use the SEAI solar calculator to estimate what a system could generate at your address
actions.desc: The free tool at seai.ie takes about five minutes and gives you a personalised estimate of generation, savings, and grant eligibility.
actions.carbon: Planning step toward ~1 tonne CO2 saving per year

actions.title: Look into a community energy project if solar is not right for your home
actions.desc: Not every home is suitable for rooftop solar. Community energy projects allow groups to share the benefits of renewables without individual rooftop installation. Visit communitypower.ie.
actions.carbon: Supports renewable energy in your community

challenges.resources: SEAI Solar PV: seai.ie/grants/solar-electricity | Community Power: communitypower.ie | International Day of the Sun: isec.org

challenges.intro_fact: One of the most exciting developments in Ireland's energy transition is the growth of community energy projects. Rather than waiting for a large company to build a wind farm nearby, communities are coming together to own their own renewable energy assets. Community energy schemes allow local people to share the financial and environmental benefits directly.

questions.text: What is a Renewable Energy Community?
options: A government scheme giving free electricity to low-income households
A local initiative where residents or groups collectively own and benefit from renewable energy generation
A solar farm built by a large private company
An EU scheme to insulate community buildings
questions.fact: Renewable Energy Communities involve groups of citizens jointly owning or investing in renewable energy infrastructure, sharing in the energy and financial benefits. The EU Renewable Energy Directive gives citizens the legal right to form them.

questions.text: What EU regulation gives citizens the right to form energy communities and sell electricity to each other?
options: The EU Renewable Energy Directive (RED II / RED III)
questions.fact: The EU Renewable Energy Directive gives citizens the legal right to form Renewable Energy Communities and participate in the energy market, including selling surplus energy and sharing it between members.

questions.text: Which Irish platform supports the development of community energy projects?
questions.fact: Community Power is Ireland's dedicated platform supporting community-owned renewable energy projects, helping groups navigate planning, grid connection, and funding for local wind and solar initiatives.

challenges.action_intro: Community energy is one of the most empowering parts of the clean energy transition. It keeps money in local communities and gives people direct ownership of the shift to renewables.

actions.title: Check if there is a community energy project in your area
actions.desc: Visit communitypower.ie to find active projects near you or explore how to start one. Community groups, GAA clubs, and housing estates have all successfully launched projects.
actions.carbon: Community renewables displace fossil fuel generation

actions.title: Share this challenge with a neighbour and start a conversation about community energy
actions.desc: Most community energy projects started with one person asking one neighbour a question. You do not need technical expertise -- just curiosity and a willingness to start.

challenges.resources: Community Power Ireland: communitypower.ie | SEAI Community Energy: seai.ie/community-energy | EU Energy Communities: energy.ec.europa.eu

challenges.intro_fact: Transport is Ireland's second biggest source of greenhouse gas emissions after agriculture. In 2024, 93% of Ireland's transport energy still came from fossil fuels. Electric vehicles are one part of the solution. But private car use remains dominant and charging infrastructure is still catching up outside major cities.

questions.text: What share of Ireland's transport energy still came from fossil fuels in 2024?
questions.fact: Overall, 93.0% of Ireland's transport energy came from fossil fuels in 2024, highlighting how far decarbonisation of transport still has to go. This is the sector where Ireland has made the least progress.

questions.text: By what year has the EU agreed to ban the sale of new petrol and diesel cars?
questions.fact: The EU has agreed that from 2035, all new cars and vans sold in the EU must be zero-emission, effectively ending the sale of new petrol and diesel cars within the EU from that date.

questions.text: What incentive is available in Ireland to help individuals buy electric vehicles through SEAI?
options: A 50% reduction in motor tax for one year
A VRT relief and purchase grant for private buyers
Free EV charging for five years
A fuel credit transferred to a new EV account
questions.fact: Ireland offers a VRT relief and a purchase grant for electric vehicles through SEAI and Revenue. Always check the current SEAI grants page for the latest figures as these are updated regularly.

challenges.action_intro: Transport is one of the hardest parts of Ireland's emissions challenge, but also one of the most visible. Every electric vehicle on the road, every bus trip, every cycle makes a difference.

actions.title: If you are due to change your car in the next two years, research EV options now
actions.desc: Use the SEAI EV grant calculator at seai.ie/grants/electric-vehicles to see what support is available. The range and charging network have improved significantly in recent years.
actions.carbon: Switching to EV saves ~2 tonnes CO2 per year vs petrol

actions.title: Try using public transport or a bicycle for one car journey this week
actions.desc: The most sustainable vehicle is the one you do not use. Even replacing one car journey per week with public transport or cycling adds up to a significant annual saving.

challenges.resources: SEAI Electric Vehicles: seai.ie/grants/electric-vehicles | Zero Emissions Vehicles Ireland: gov.ie | Transport for Ireland: transportforireland.ie

challenges.intro_fact: It is the end of June and we are halfway through 2026. This month we explored ocean health, Ireland's energy transition, cycling, rainforests, peatlands, and the urgent gap between climate targets and reality. Ireland's emissions are still well off track to meet its 2030 target of 51% reduction. Missing that target could cost the country between EUR 3 billion and EUR 26 billion in emissions allowances. The second half of the year is an opportunity to close that gap.

questions.text: Which of the following is the single biggest source of greenhouse gas emissions in Ireland?
questions.fact: Agriculture is consistently Ireland's largest single source of greenhouse gas emissions, accounting for around 37% of national emissions, primarily from livestock methane and fertiliser use. It is the most challenging sector to decarbonise.

questions.text: The Paris Agreement aims to limit global temperature rise to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels. By how much has the global average temperature already risen?
questions.fact: The World Meteorological Organisation confirmed 2024 as the warmest year on record, with the global average temperature crossing the 1.5C threshold set by the Paris Agreement for the first time.

questions.text: If Ireland fails to meet its EU Effort Sharing Regulation targets, what is the likely financial consequence?
options: A symbolic fine with no real cost
Ireland would need to purchase emissions allowances from other EU member states at an estimated cost of EUR 3 to EUR 26 billion
Ireland would have to leave the EU Emissions Trading System
questions.fact: Current projections indicate Ireland will need to purchase substantial emissions allowances from other member states at an estimated cost of EUR 3 billion to EUR 26 billion -- money that could be invested in the transition instead.

challenges.action_intro: Knowledge without action is just information. The second half of 2026 is your opportunity. July brings Plastic Free July -- a ready-made challenge to start with.

actions.title: Write down one thing you have changed or learned about sustainability in the first half of 2026
actions.desc: Even a single note in your phone counts. Reflecting on what you have done so far makes it more likely you will keep going. Progress, not perfection.

actions.title: Sign up for Plastic Free July starting next week
actions.desc: Visit plasticfreejuly.org and choose your level of challenge for July. The campaign has over 100 million participants and makes it much easier to cut single-use plastic when you are doing it alongside millions of others.
actions.carbon: Reduces single-use plastic consumption throughout July

challenges.resources: EPA Climate Action data: epa.ie | Plastic Free July: plasticfreejuly.org | Climate Action Ireland: climateaction.ie

challenges.intro_fact: July is here, and so is Plastic Free July -- one of the most successful global behaviour change campaigns in the world. Started in Australia in 2011, it now reaches over 100 million people in more than 190 countries. The challenge is simple: refuse single-use plastic for the month. You do not have to be perfect. Even cutting out the top four -- plastic bottles, bags, straws, and coffee cup lids -- makes a real difference.

questions.text: When did the Plastic Free July challenge first begin?
questions.fact: Plastic Free July was started in 2011 by the Plastic Free Foundation in Australia, beginning as a small local campaign and growing into one of the world's largest voluntary environmental movements.

questions.text: Approximately how many people globally participate in Plastic Free July each year?
questions.fact: Plastic Free July has grown to reach over 100 million participants across more than 190 countries, making it one of the largest voluntary environmental campaigns on the planet.

questions.text: How much plastic does humanity produce globally each year?
questions.fact: Humanity produces more than 400 million tonnes of plastic each year, much of which ends up in the environment. Only around 9% of all plastic ever produced has been recycled.

challenges.action_intro: You do not have to be perfect to make a difference. Pick one type of single-use plastic to refuse this month and start there.

actions.title: Sign up for the official Plastic Free July challenge
actions.desc: Visit plasticfreejuly.org -- it is free, takes one minute, and connects you to over 100 million people doing the same thing. Choose your level: one item, the top four, or all single-use plastic.
actions.carbon: Commits you to a month of reduced plastic use

actions.title: Tell one other person about Plastic Free July today
actions.desc: Behaviour change is easier when you do it with someone else. Tell a friend, colleague, or family member and invite them to join you.

challenges.resources: Plastic Free July: plasticfreejuly.org | Clean Coasts Ireland: cleancoasts.org | My Waste Ireland: mywaste.ie

challenges.intro_fact: Ireland has over 2,500 kilometres of coastline -- one of our greatest national treasures. But plastic pollution is washing up on those shores every day, carried by wind, rain, rivers, and tides. Between 70 and 80% of ocean plastic starts on land. What we drop in a car park in Dublin can end up on a beach in Connemara.

questions.text: What percentage of plastic in the ocean comes from land-based sources rather than directly from ships or fishing?
questions.fact: Between 70 and 80% of plastic in the ocean comes from land-based sources, including littering, poorly managed waste, and runoff from rivers and drainage systems. What happens on land reaches the sea.

questions.text: What measurable impact did Ireland's Deposit Return Scheme have on marine litter by the end of 2024?
options: No impact was recorded in the first year
Bottle and can litter on Irish shores fell to the lowest average in 25 years
Marine litter increased because other types replaced bottles and cans
It reduced marine litter by 10% overall
questions.fact: The Coastwatch Annual Marine Litter Survey found 2024 recorded the lowest average levels of bottle and can litter on Irish shores in 25 years, directly following the introduction of the Deposit Return Scheme.

questions.text: By 2025, how much had bottle and can litter dropped in Irish towns and cities compared to before the Deposit Return Scheme?
questions.fact: By 2025, plastic bottles and cans were 60% less common as litter in Irish towns and cities compared to when the Deposit Return Scheme was introduced in early 2024. It is one of the most measurable environmental policy wins in recent Irish history.

challenges.action_intro: The Deposit Return Scheme shows that policy works when people use it. Return your bottles, pick up litter near water, and keep Ireland's coastline clean.

actions.title: Return your plastic bottles and cans this week
actions.desc: Use the Re-Turn app or website to find your nearest return point. You get your deposit back, and the materials stay in the circular economy and out of the ocean.
actions.carbon: Reduces plastic entering the marine environment

actions.title: Pick up three pieces of litter on your next walk near water
actions.desc: It takes 30 seconds and removes potential marine pollution directly. Rivers, canals, and coastal paths are where land-based plastic most often enters the sea.

challenges.resources: Re-Turn Ireland: re-turn.ie | Clean Coasts: cleancoasts.org | IBAL litter reports: ibal.ie

challenges.intro_fact: Today is International Plastic Bag Free Day. In 2002, Ireland became the first country in the world to impose a plastic bag levy. That single policy decision -- a 15 cent charge on plastic shopping bags -- caused a near-overnight transformation. It is one of the most studied and copied environmental policies in history, and it started here.

questions.text: What year did Ireland introduce the world's first plastic bag levy?
questions.fact: Ireland's plastic bag levy was introduced on 4 March 2002, making it the first country in the world to charge consumers for single-use plastic shopping bags at point of sale.

questions.text: Before the levy, how many plastic bags were given out free in Irish shops every year?
questions.fact: Prior to the levy, over 1.2 billion plastic bags were dispensed free of charge at Irish retail outlets annually -- roughly 328 bags per person per year. Within months of the levy, that number collapsed by around 90%.

questions.text: Plastic bag litter made up 5% of Ireland's national litter before the levy. What did it fall to by 2004?
options: It had not changed significantly by 2004
questions.fact: Before the levy, plastic bags accounted for 5% of litter in Ireland. By 2004, this had dropped to 0.22%. The Irish policy has since been copied across Europe, Africa, and many US states.

challenges.action_intro: Ireland proved that the right policy, applied simply, can change behaviour almost overnight. The same approach is now being applied to bottles, cups, and packaging.

actions.title: Count how many single-use plastic bags come into your home this week
actions.desc: Just count them. Awareness is the first step. Then aim to cut that number in half next week by keeping a reusable bag in your car, bag, or coat pocket.
actions.carbon: Builds awareness of personal plastic use

actions.title: Share Ireland's plastic bag levy story with someone outside Ireland
actions.desc: Most people outside Ireland do not know it started here. It is a great example of a policy that actually worked and a conversation starter about what is possible.

challenges.resources: Plastic Bag Levy history: irishenvironment.com | MARLISCO case study: marlisco.eu | Plastic Free July: plasticfreejuly.org

challenges.intro_fact: When you buy something -- food, cleaning products, toiletries -- it usually comes in packaging. In Ireland, a huge amount of that packaging is plastic. Reducing packaging in the first place is always better than recycling it. And the EU is shifting the cost of packaging waste from taxpayers to the businesses that create it.

questions.text: In Ireland, what is Repak?
options: A government agency that manages recycling bins
Ireland's approved packaging compliance scheme through which businesses fund recovery and recycling
A European Union packaging labelling system
A not-for-profit that runs community recycling events
questions.fact: Repak is Ireland's sole approved body for packaging compliance, requiring producers to finance the collection and recycling of all packaging they place on the Irish market. In 2026, Repak was granted a new 10-year licence.

questions.text: What does Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) mean in the context of packaging?
options: Consumers are responsible for sorting all their own recycling
Retailers pay extra tax on all imported goods
The businesses that create or import packaging are financially responsible for its collection and recycling
The government takes full responsibility for all packaging waste costs
questions.fact: Extended Producer Responsibility requires that producers, not taxpayers, pay for the recovery and recycling of the packaging they place on the market. Ireland operates this through Repak, covering over 3,000 member companies.

questions.text: Ireland's plastic packaging recycling target under EU rules is 50% by 2025, rising to what in 2030?
questions.fact: Ireland must achieve a plastic packaging recycling rate of 55% by 2030 under the EU Waste Framework Directive. Meeting this target requires both better consumer sorting and better packaging design from producers.

challenges.action_intro: The best packaging is the one that was never made. When buying this week, ask whether you actually need the packaging that comes with it.

actions.title: Choose loose fruit and vegetables instead of pre-packaged ones this week
actions.desc: Loose produce is almost always available in Irish supermarkets and costs the same or less. It is one of the simplest packaging reductions you can make every single week.

actions.title: Check mywaste.ie before putting something in the recycling bin
actions.desc: Not all plastic is recyclable. Black plastic trays, crisp packets, and stretchy film cannot go in the household recycling. Check before you bin.

challenges.resources: Repak Ireland: repak.ie | My Waste recycling guide: mywaste.ie | EPA single-use plastics: epa.ie/plastics

challenges.intro_fact: Today is World Temperate Rainforest Day. Ireland holds a truly global rarity: ancient Atlantic rainforest. Most people are surprised to learn this. In places like Killarney, Uragh Wood, Glengarriff, and north into Donegal, fragments of a forest that once covered 80% of Ireland still survive. They are draped in mosses, liverworts, and ferns of extraordinary diversity -- one of the richest habitats in Europe.

questions.text: What is the main reason Ireland's western woodlands qualify as temperate rainforest?
options: They contain tropical tree species brought by the Gulf Stream
They experience very high rainfall and mild temperatures, supporting rich communities of mosses and ferns
They are taller than normal forests due to coastal winds
They are found below sea level, keeping them permanently moist
questions.fact: Ireland's temperate rainforests are defined by high rainfall, mild Atlantic temperatures, and the richness of mosses, liverworts, and ferns that grow on the trees themselves, making them the country's richest terrestrial habitat.

questions.text: How much of Ireland was covered by this type of ancient forest before humans arrived approximately 7,000 years ago?
questions.fact: Ancient damp-climate oceanic forest once covered an estimated 80% of Ireland before the arrival of humans. Today only small fragments survive, mostly along the western seaboard in national parks.

questions.text: What is the main threat to Ireland's remaining temperate rainforest fragments today?
options: Rising temperatures drying out the habitat
Deer overgrazing, invasive rhododendron, and the absence of large predators to control deer numbers
Coastal flooding due to sea level rise
questions.fact: Ireland's remaining rainforest fragments face serious threats from sika deer overgrazing and invasive rhododendron, which chokes out native woodland regeneration. The absence of wolves and other large predators means deer go unchecked.

challenges.action_intro: Ireland's rainforest is one of the world's great ecological secrets. Visiting it, talking about it, and supporting its restoration are all meaningful actions.

actions.title: Support the Wild Atlantic Rainforest Restoration Project
actions.desc: Visit hometree.ie to learn about rainforest restoration in Ireland and plant a native tree. Oak, birch, and hazel are all part of the ancient rainforest and can be planted in gardens.
actions.carbon: Native woodland restoration stores carbon and supports biodiversity

actions.title: Share the fact that Ireland has rainforest with one person today
actions.desc: Most Irish people have never heard of temperate rainforest. Sharing the story builds awareness and support for conservation. You can start by sharing today's challenge.
actions.carbon: Builds awareness of Ireland's rarest habitat

challenges.resources: Hometree Wild Atlantic Rainforest: hometree.ie | Irish Wildlife Trust: iwt.ie | NPWS woodland habitats: npws.ie

challenges.intro_fact: Most of us worry about plastic bottles and bags. But there is a more invisible plastic problem growing around us. Microplastics are tiny particles smaller than 5mm, now found everywhere -- in our water, our soil, our food, and our bodies. A 2024 study found them in arterial plaques. Researchers found them in breast milk, lungs, and kidneys.

questions.text: What is the definition of a microplastic?
options: Any plastic item smaller than a bottle cap
A synthetic polymer particle smaller than 5mm that does not biodegrade
A biodegradable alternative to single-use plastic
Plastic that has been chemically treated to dissolve in water
questions.fact: Microplastics are synthetic polymer particles below five millimetres that are insoluble and resist degradation. They come from plastics breaking down in the environment and from products like synthetic clothing and tyres.

questions.text: Where in the human body have microplastics now been detected?
options: Only in blood samples from urban areas
In the lungs, blood, liver, kidneys, placenta, and breast milk
Only in the skin surface layer
questions.fact: Traces of microplastics have been detected in human placentas, lung tissue, breast milk, saliva, blood, liver, kidneys, and the colon. A 2024 study in The Lancet found them in arterial plaques, linked to higher cardiovascular risk.

questions.text: The EU has set a target to reduce microplastic releases into the environment by 2030. What is that target?
questions.fact: The EU Zero Pollution Action Plan sets a 30% reduction target for microplastic releases into the environment by 2030, with the EU leading global efforts to regulate and restrict intentionally added microplastics.

challenges.action_intro: Microplastics are in our bodies and our environment. Reducing the plastic we use now reduces the microplastics of the future.

actions.title: Wash synthetic clothing less frequently and at lower temperatures
actions.desc: Synthetic fibres like polyester and nylon shed microplastics with every wash. Washing at 30C less often significantly reduces the amount released into waterways.
actions.carbon: Reduces microplastic pollution and energy use

actions.title: Check personal care products for microbeads using the Beat the Microbead app
actions.desc: Download the free Beat the Microbead app (beatthemicrobead.org) to scan products and identify those containing intentionally added plastic particles.

challenges.resources: Beat the Microbead: beatthemicrobead.org | EU Microplastics policy: environment.ec.europa.eu | Clean Coasts Ireland: cleancoasts.org

challenges.intro_fact: Plastic Free July does not require you to overhaul your entire life. Focusing on the top four single-use plastics -- bottles, bags, coffee cups, and food packaging -- covers the vast majority of everyday plastic waste. Small changes made consistently across millions of people add up to something genuinely significant.

questions.text: Which of the following is the single most common form of litter found in Irish towns and cities in 2025?
questions.fact: Cigarette butts remain the most common litter item in Irish towns, present in 31% of all sites surveyed in IBAL's January 2026 report, while coffee cups were found in one fifth of all sites.

questions.text: A reusable coffee cup needs to be used approximately how many times before it offsets the environmental cost of making it?
questions.fact: A reusable coffee cup needs to be used around 15 to 20 times to offset the higher carbon cost of its manufacture compared to a single-use cup. After that, each use saves emissions significantly.

questions.text: Ireland promised a levy on disposable coffee cups. As of early 2026, what was the status of this levy?
options: It was introduced in January 2025 and is now in full operation
It was still being delayed, frustrating environmental groups
It was rejected by the Oireachtas
It applies only to plastic-lined cups
questions.fact: A coffee cup levy was promised years ago but continued to be delayed, with IBAL calling the Government's lack of action 'striking' in January 2026 given that coffee cups remained one of the most common litter items across Ireland.

challenges.action_intro: You do not need to do everything. Pick the one swap that is most relevant to your daily routine and focus on that for the rest of July.

actions.title: Bring your reusable coffee cup every day this week
actions.desc: Put it next to your keys or bag tonight so you cannot leave without it tomorrow. If you forget it, skip the takeaway coffee -- that is the challenge.
actions.carbon: Removes ~365 disposable cups per year from circulation

actions.title: Refuse a straw, lid, or single-use cutlery you do not need this week
actions.desc: When ordering food or a drink, simply say you do not need the straw or plastic lid. One word saves one item of plastic every time.

challenges.resources: Plastic Free July swaps guide: plasticfreejuly.org | My Waste Ireland: mywaste.ie | IBAL litter reports: ibal.ie

challenges.intro_fact: Food packaging is the single largest category of plastic use in Ireland and across Europe. In 2022 alone, over 3,000 tonnes of plastic food containers were placed on the Irish market. Some packaging has a genuine purpose -- keeping food safe and reducing food waste. But a lot of it is unnecessary, and the EU is now requiring change.

questions.text: What is the EU's target for all plastic packaging on the EU market to be recyclable?
questions.fact: Under the EU Plastics Strategy, all plastic packaging on the EU market must be recyclable by 2030, with single-use plastic consumption reduced and microplastics restricted.

questions.text: The EU Single-Use Plastics Directive set a specific 2026 requirement for member states. What is it?
options: A ban on all plastic food containers
Each member state must demonstrate measurable reductions in consumption of key single-use plastic products compared to 2022 levels
A 50% recycled content requirement for all beverage packaging
A ban on plastic packaging for fresh produce
questions.fact: From 2026, each EU Member State must demonstrate measurable reductions in the consumption of key single-use plastic products compared with 2022 baseline levels -- making 2026 a significant year for plastic policy.

questions.text: The EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation requires businesses in the food sector to do what by 2030?
options: Consumers must be offered a reusable or refillable option when purchasing takeaway food and drinks
Takeaway packaging must contain at least 50% recycled content
Disposable cups must carry a health warning
questions.fact: From 2030, businesses offering takeaway food and drinks must offer consumers a reusable or refillable option under the EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation -- a structural shift away from single-use packaging.

challenges.action_intro: The EU is changing the rules. Consumers can accelerate it by choosing businesses and products that are already ahead of the law.

actions.title: Choose loose fruit and vegetables instead of pre-packaged options this weekend
