actions.desc: Most Irish supermarkets stock loose produce that is the same quality and price as packaged alternatives. Making this swap every week removes a significant amount of packaging over a year.

actions.title: Bring your own container to a deli or takeaway that allows it
actions.desc: Many Irish delis and cafes now accept customer containers. Ask first -- most are happy to oblige and some offer a small discount.

challenges.resources: EPA Single-Use Plastics: epa.ie/plastics | My Waste Ireland: mywaste.ie | EU Single-Use Plastics Directive: environment.ec.europa.eu

challenges.intro_fact: One of the most common reasons people give for not doing Plastic Free July is that they think it is impossible in an Irish supermarket. That is less true than it used to be. Refill shops, farmers markets, zero-waste stores, and package-free options in mainstream supermarkets have all grown. And EU law now requires businesses to offer reusable options.

questions.text: Which of the following is a good place to shop with less plastic packaging in Ireland?
options: A farmers market, zero-waste shop, or the loose produce section of a supermarket
Online delivery services where packaging is unavoidable
questions.fact: Farmers markets, zero-waste refill shops, and loose produce sections of supermarkets offer practical ways to reduce packaging in everyday shopping. Several Irish towns now have dedicated zero-waste shops.

questions.text: Ireland's Deposit Return Scheme aims to achieve a specific collection rate for plastic bottles by 2029. What is that target?
questions.fact: The EU Single-Use Plastics Directive requires a 90% separate collection rate for plastic beverage bottles by 2029, supported by deposit return schemes. Ireland's scheme already collected 76% in its first full year.

questions.text: The EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation requires businesses offering takeaway to offer reusable options by what year?
questions.fact: From 2030, businesses offering takeaway food and drinks must offer consumers a reusable or refillable option under the EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation -- a structural shift that is already beginning in Ireland.

challenges.action_intro: Shopping without plastic is increasingly possible in Ireland. This week, try doing it for at least one shop.

actions.title: Find your nearest zero-waste or refill shop
actions.desc: Search 'zero waste shop' with your town name. Many Irish towns now have them. Try buying one product -- washing-up liquid, shampoo, or oats -- without packaging this week.

actions.title: Try one meal this week using only ingredients without plastic packaging
actions.desc: Plan a meal using loose produce, glass jars, or tins. Pasta with tomatoes from a glass jar and loose onions and garlic is a good starting point.

challenges.resources: Plastic Free July shop guide: plasticfreejuly.org | Re-Turn Deposit Return Scheme: re-turn.ie | Zero Waste Ireland: zerowasteireland.ie

challenges.intro_fact: Since July 2021, a number of single-use plastic products can no longer be sold legally in Ireland or anywhere in the EU. The EU Single-Use Plastics Directive targeted the ten most common plastic items found on European beaches. It was a significant step. But it was also just a first step.

questions.text: Which of the following items was banned from the Irish market under the EU Single-Use Plastics Directive since July 2021?
options: Plastic cotton bud sticks, cutlery, plates, straws, and balloon sticks
questions.fact: Since July 2021, single-use plastic cotton bud sticks, cutlery, plates, stirrers, balloon sticks, and straws can no longer be placed on the market in Ireland under the EU Single-Use Plastics Directive.

questions.text: From July 2024, a new design requirement came in for plastic beverage bottles sold in the EU. What was it?
options: Bottles must be made from at least 25% recycled content
Bottle caps must remain attached to the container during use
Bottles must carry a QR code linking to recycling instructions
All bottles over 1 litre must be made from glass or metal
questions.fact: From July 2024, plastic beverage bottle caps must remain attached to the container during use, preventing caps from being discarded separately and ending up in the environment. That is why your bottle cap now stays tethered.

questions.text: What percentage of all plastic ever produced globally has actually been recycled?
questions.fact: Only around 9% of all plastics ever produced have been recycled globally. Around 12% have been incinerated and the rest remains in use, in landfill, or in the natural environment.

challenges.action_intro: The EU bans are progress. But they only cover a small fraction of the plastic we use. Consumer choices fill the gap that law has not yet reached.

actions.title: Check your bathroom cabinet for products containing microbeads
actions.desc: Look for 'polyethylene' or 'polypropylene' in the ingredients list of scrubs, toothpaste, or face washes. If present, switch to a product without them. Use the Beat the Microbead app to scan products.

actions.title: Write to your local supermarket asking them to expand loose or refillable options
actions.desc: Supermarkets respond to customer feedback. A short email asking for more loose produce or refill stations takes five minutes and contributes to retail change.

challenges.resources: EPA Single-Use Plastics in Ireland: epa.ie/plastics | EU Directive overview: environment.ec.europa.eu | Voice Ireland: voiceireland.org

challenges.intro_fact: Ireland has made real progress on litter in recent years. The Deposit Return Scheme has been a genuine success. But litter remains a problem across our towns, cities, and coastlines. Coffee cups, cigarette butts, and sweet wrappers are stubbornly common. Litter is not just ugly -- it costs money to clean up, it damages tourism, and it harms wildlife.

questions.text: In the IBAL January 2026 survey, how many of 40 Irish towns and cities were rated as clean?
questions.fact: In IBAL's January 2026 survey, 28 of the 40 towns and cities surveyed were deemed clean, a rise on 2024, with Sligo finishing top of the rankings for the first time. Progress is real but uneven.

questions.text: One year after Ireland's Deposit Return Scheme launched, plastic bottle and can litter had fallen by approximately how much?
questions.fact: One year after the Deposit Return Scheme launched, plastic bottle and can litter had fallen by approximately 50% in Irish towns and cities -- one of the fastest improvements in litter levels in Irish history.

questions.text: As of early 2026, what was the most commonly littered item in Irish city areas despite a promised government levy?
questions.fact: Coffee cups remained one of the most commonly found forms of litter across Ireland in 2025, found in one fifth of all sites surveyed. A promised government levy on disposable cups had still not been introduced by early 2026.

challenges.action_intro: Litter is a solvable problem. It requires both policy action and individual behaviour. You can influence both.

actions.title: Carry a reusable cup today
actions.desc: If you are going to a coffee shop, bring your cup. If you forget it, drink in rather than taking away. One cup per day adds up to around 250 disposable cups per year.
actions.carbon: Removes ~250 disposable cups per year from circulation

actions.title: Report a litter blackspot in your area
actions.desc: Contact your local council or use the Litter.ie reporting tool. Local authorities are required to respond to litter reports. Your report matters.

challenges.resources: IBAL (Irish Business Against Litter): ibal.ie | An Taisce Green Schools: greenschoolsireland.org | Clean Coasts: cleancoasts.org

challenges.intro_fact: Most of us put plastic into the recycling bin and assume it gets recycled. The reality is more complicated. Not all plastic is recyclable. Not all recyclable plastic actually gets recycled. And even when it does, most plastic can only be recycled a limited number of times before it degrades. Reducing plastic in the first place is always more effective than recycling it.

questions.text: Which of these plastic items is generally NOT recyclable in the standard Irish household recycling bin?
questions.fact: Black plastic food trays are generally not recyclable in Ireland because the carbon-black pigment cannot be detected by sorting equipment in recycling facilities. Always check mywaste.ie for current guidance.

questions.text: Globally, what percentage of all plastic ever produced has actually been recycled?
questions.fact: Only around 9% of all plastics ever produced have been recycled globally. Around 12% have been incinerated and the rest remains in use, in landfill, or in the natural environment including the ocean.

questions.text: In Ireland, rigid plastic packaging such as PET bottles is typically recycled into what?
options: All recycled plastic stays in Ireland and is turned back into the same packaging
Recycled plastic is mostly exported to China
Polyester fibres for clothing and PET trays for fresh produce
All plastic collected in Irish bins is used to generate energy locally
questions.fact: In Ireland, rigid plastic packaging such as PET bottles is processed into polyester fibres for clothing and PET trays for fresh produce. Flexible plastic is far more complicated to collect and recycle.

challenges.action_intro: Recycling is important but it is the last resort, not the first. Reduce and refuse first, then recycle what cannot be avoided.

actions.title: Before you bin something today, check mywaste.ie to make sure it belongs in recycling
actions.desc: One contaminated load can cause an entire truck of recycling to go to landfill. Checking takes 30 seconds and makes the recycling system work properly.

actions.title: Rinse containers before putting them in the recycling bin
actions.desc: Food residue contaminates other materials in the recycling stream. A quick rinse of yogurt pots, sauce jars, and tins is all that is needed.

challenges.resources: My Waste Ireland: mywaste.ie | Repak recycling guide: repak.ie | EPA Packaging and Waste: epa.ie

challenges.intro_fact: We are at the midpoint of Plastic Free July. Whether you have stuck fully to your challenge or stumbled a few times, you are more aware of plastic than you were two weeks ago. That awareness is the first step. Research shows that people who complete even part of Plastic Free July maintain lower plastic use for months afterwards.

questions.text: Research on Plastic Free July participants shows that people who take part tend to do what after the month ends?
options: Go back to their old habits immediately
Maintain reduced plastic use for months or years afterwards
Increase their plastic use because of the discipline required
Show no measurable change in long-term behaviour
questions.fact: Research by the Plastic Free Foundation shows that the majority of participants maintain positive behaviour changes after the challenge ends, including continuing to refuse single-use plastic and choosing reusable alternatives.

questions.text: A 2024 study published in The Lancet Planetary Health found microplastics in what proportion of patients with carotid artery disease who then experienced cardiovascular events?
questions.fact: A 2024 Italian study found polypropylene microplastics in 58.4% of patients' arterial plaques, with those who had detectable microplastics showing a significantly higher risk of heart attack and stroke.

questions.text: The EU has set a target to reduce microplastic releases by 30% by 2030. What is the EU policy framework that contains this target?
options: EU Circular Economy Action Plan only
questions.fact: The EU Zero Pollution Action Plan sets a 30% reduction target for microplastic releases into the environment by 2030, as part of a broader ambition to reach zero pollution across air, water, and soil.

challenges.action_intro: Progress, not perfection. Take five minutes today to reflect on what you have changed this month and what you want to carry forward into August.

actions.title: Write down which plastic swaps you have managed to make this month
actions.desc: Even a note in your phone counts. Reflecting on what you have done makes it more likely you will keep going after July ends.

actions.title: Share your Plastic Free July experience with one person
actions.desc: Tell someone what you have changed this month. Research shows that talking about behaviour change with others is one of the most effective ways to sustain it.

challenges.resources: Plastic Free July: plasticfreejuly.org | The Lancet Planetary Health: thelancet.com | Clean Coasts Ireland: cleancoasts.org

challenges.intro_fact: Most conversations about plastic focus on packaging and litter. But agriculture is a major and often overlooked source of plastic waste. Irish farms use enormous amounts of plastic every year: silage wrap, bale netting, polytunnels, pesticide containers, and feed bags. Much of this agricultural plastic ends up burned, buried, or abandoned in rural areas.

questions.text: What is the main source of agricultural plastic waste on Irish farms?
options: Plastic water bottles used by farm workers
Silage wrap and bale netting used to preserve winter fodder
Plastic packaging from imported farm machinery
Single-use plastic gloves used in animal husbandry
questions.fact: Silage stretch wrap and bale netting are the dominant sources of plastic waste on Irish farms, used in very large quantities to preserve grass silage as winter feed for livestock.

questions.text: What is the recommended approach for farmers managing agricultural plastic in Ireland?
options: Burn agricultural plastic on-farm to reduce volume
Bury agricultural plastic in unused corners of the farm
Clean and return agricultural plastic to licensed collection points for recycling
Mix agricultural plastic with household recycling
questions.fact: Farmers are encouraged to clean and return agricultural plastics to licensed collection points. Several county-level collection schemes operate across Ireland, and Repak operates agricultural plastic take-back programmes.

questions.text: The EU Single-Use Plastics Directive also covers plastic used in what sector beyond consumer products?
questions.fact: The EU Single-Use Plastics Directive also addresses fishing gear and plastic used in agriculture, committing EU member states to introduce measures to manage these materials and reduce their environmental impact.

challenges.action_intro: Agricultural plastic is an invisible part of Ireland's plastic problem. Understanding it and supporting good practice on farms is part of solving it.

actions.title: If you know a farmer, ask how agricultural plastic is managed on their farm
actions.desc: It starts a useful conversation and may help a farmer find options they were not aware of, such as county collection schemes or Repak take-back programmes.
actions.carbon: Raises awareness of agricultural plastic waste

actions.title: Avoid buying products that use excessive secondary plastic packaging
actions.desc: Secondary packaging -- shrink wrap, plastic trays holding multiple items -- is one of the least necessary forms. Choosing products without it sends a market signal to producers.

challenges.resources: Teagasc environmental guidance: teagasc.ie | EPA agricultural plastic: epa.ie | Repak agricultural plastic: repak.ie

challenges.intro_fact: Plastic pollution is one of those problems where it is tempting to blame someone else. Consumers blame companies. Companies blame consumers. The truth is that responsibility is shared -- and the EU is increasingly placing the financial and legal burden on the producers of plastic products. Meanwhile, individuals still have real power through their daily choices.

questions.text: What does the 'Green Dot' symbol on packaging in Ireland mean?
options: The packaging is made from 100% recycled material
The producer has contributed financially to a packaging recovery scheme such as Repak
The packaging can be placed in any Irish recycling bin
questions.fact: The Green Dot symbol indicates that the producer has contributed financially to packaging recovery. It does not guarantee that the packaging itself is recyclable or has been recycled.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of greenwashing on a plastic product?
options: A product labelled 'made from 30% recycled plastic' when verified
A product labelled 'eco-friendly' or 'biodegradable' without specifying conditions or timeframes
A product that carries the Green Dot symbol
A product labelled 'widely recycled in Ireland'
questions.fact: Vague claims like 'biodegradable' or 'eco-friendly' without specified conditions are a common form of greenwashing. The EU Green Claims Directive being developed will require that environmental claims are independently verified and specific.

questions.text: Repak's Plastic Pledge commits how many major Irish producers to cutting single-use plastic?
questions.fact: Repak's Plastic Pledge has been signed by more than 140 major Irish producers, committing them to cutting single-use plastic and improving the recyclability of their packaging as part of Ireland's Extended Producer Responsibility framework.

challenges.action_intro: Producers are responsible. Governments are responsible. And so are we. The most powerful thing consumers can do is make the responsible choice visible and consistent.

actions.title: When you see 'biodegradable' on a product, ask what conditions are required
actions.desc: Most 'biodegradable' plastics only biodegrade in industrial composting facilities, not in home compost or the environment. If the conditions are not specified, treat the claim with scepticism.

actions.title: Write to one brand you buy from asking what they are doing to reduce single-use plastic
actions.desc: Companies track customer feedback. A short email from a customer carries more weight than you might think, especially when combined with others asking the same question.

challenges.resources: Repak and Green Dot: repak.ie | EU Green Claims Directive: environment.ec.europa.eu | VOICE Ireland: voiceireland.org

challenges.intro_fact: The most sustainable plastic is the one that does not exist. The second most sustainable is one used dozens or hundreds of times. Refill and reuse systems are growing across Ireland and Europe, driven by consumer demand and new EU law. From refillable cleaning products to public water stations, the infrastructure is building.

questions.text: What does a refill station in a shop allow customers to do?
options: Return empty plastic bottles for a cash refund
Bring their own containers to fill with products like cleaning liquids, shampoo, or oils
Drop off single-use plastic for incineration
Print recycling labels for their home packaging
questions.fact: Refill stations allow customers to bring reusable containers and fill them with everyday products, eliminating the need for new single-use packaging with every purchase. They are now available in several Irish towns.

questions.text: Which app helps people find public water refill points in Ireland?
questions.fact: Apps including Refill.ie and the global Tap app allow users to find free public water refill points, helping people avoid buying single-use plastic water bottles when out and about in Irish towns and cities.

questions.text: The EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation sets ambitious reuse targets for which sector by 2030?
options: The food and beverage takeaway sector
questions.fact: The EU PPWR sets particularly strong reuse and refill targets for the food and beverage takeaway sector, requiring that from 2030 consumers must be offered a reusable alternative when purchasing takeaway food or drinks.

challenges.action_intro: Refill and reuse are not niche alternatives. They are the direction the entire system is moving. Getting ahead of it now makes your life easier later.

actions.title: Find your nearest refill shop and try buying one product without packaging
actions.desc: Search 'zero waste shop' or 'refill shop' with your town name. Many now stock washing-up liquid, shampoo, conditioner, and dry goods. Try one product this week.

actions.title: Carry a refillable water bottle this week and use a public refill point
actions.desc: Use the Tap app to find a free water refill point near you. It is free, takes no extra time, and removes one plastic bottle per use from circulation.

challenges.resources: Zero Waste Ireland: zerowasteireland.ie | Refill points Ireland: refill.ie | Plastic Free July refill guide: plasticfreejuly.org

challenges.intro_fact: Individual action matters. But businesses have far greater reach. One decision by a supermarket or a café reaches hundreds of thousands of people. In Ireland, some businesses are leading the way. Many more are still waiting for the law to require it. The EU is moving quickly, which means the pressure on businesses to act is growing fast.

questions.text: What simple action could a café or takeaway business take right now to reduce plastic use?
options: Offer a discount to customers who bring their own reusable cup or container
Switch to black plastic food containers which are more durable
Use a different colour bag to signal plastic reduction
questions.fact: Offering a discount for reusable cups or containers is one of the most effective and low-cost actions a food business can take. Many Irish cafes already do this and report high customer uptake.

questions.text: The EU Green Claims Directive, currently being developed, will require businesses to do what before making environmental claims?
options: Register the claim with a national government body
Ensure claims are independently verified and meet specific evidence standards before use in marketing
Pay a fee to use any sustainability-related label
Remove all environmental claims until the directive comes into full force
questions.fact: The EU Green Claims Directive will require that environmental claims are independently verified, specific, and meet a defined evidence standard, making it illegal to use vague terms like 'eco-friendly' without proof.

questions.text: Repak's Plastic Pledge has been signed by how many major Irish producers committing to cut single-use plastic?
questions.fact: Repak's Plastic Pledge has been signed by more than 140 major Irish producers, committing them to cutting single-use plastic and improving recyclability as part of Ireland's Extended Producer Responsibility framework.

challenges.action_intro: Business change happens faster when customers ask for it. You are a customer every day. Use that.

actions.title: Ask your workplace about its policy on single-use plastic
actions.desc: Does your canteen, office kitchen, or event catering use single-use plastic? A simple question to facilities management or the sustainability team can start a useful conversation.

actions.title: Choose to buy from one business this week that is making a genuine effort to reduce packaging
actions.desc: Vote with your wallet. Supporting businesses that have already made changes encourages others to follow. Look for reusable cup discounts, loose produce, and plastic-free shelves.

challenges.resources: Repak Plastic Pledge: repak.ie | IBEC sustainability: ibec.ie | EU Green Claims Directive: environment.ec.europa.eu

challenges.intro_fact: Today is International Self-Care Day. Spending time in nature is one of the most evidence-based forms of self-care there is. And here is the connection that often gets missed: when we feel connected to nature, we are more motivated to protect it. Looking after yourself and looking after the environment are not separate things.

questions.text: Research consistently shows that spending time in nature has what effect on stress levels?
options: A small temporary benefit during the visit only
A measurable reduction in cortisol and improved mood
A beneficial effect only in tropical or warm climates
questions.fact: Multiple peer-reviewed studies show that time in natural environments reduces cortisol levels, lowers blood pressure, and improves mood, with effects lasting beyond the visit itself.

questions.text: The Japanese practice of Shinrin-yoku, or forest bathing, involves what?
options: Swimming in mountain streams and cold-water therapy
Deliberately spending calm, mindful time among trees using all the senses
Eating foraged food from forests as a nutritional supplement
Sleeping outdoors in woodland settings for at least one week
questions.fact: Shinrin-yoku, or forest bathing, is the practice of spending slow, mindful time in forests, engaging all the senses. Research from Japan and Europe has found measurable immune, mood, and stress benefits from even short sessions.

questions.text: Which of Ireland's six national parks is the largest by area?
questions.fact: Ballycroy National Park in Mayo is Ireland's largest national park, covering approximately 11,000 hectares of blanket bog and Atlantic mountain terrain. Entry is free.

challenges.action_intro: Self-care and environmental care are the same story. This weekend, give yourself the gift of time outside.

actions.title: Plan a visit to a green space, forest, beach, or national park this weekend
actions.desc: Leave the phone behind if you can. Walk slowly. Notice what you see, hear, and smell. Research shows that even 20 minutes makes a measurable difference to your mood.
actions.carbon: Zero carbon and significant wellbeing benefit

actions.title: Invite one other person to join you outdoors
actions.desc: Connection in nature is doubly beneficial. Suggest an outdoor walk, cycle, or park visit to someone you care about this week.

challenges.resources: National Parks Ireland: npws.ie | Leave No Trace Ireland: leavenotraceireland.org | HSE Mental Health and Nature: hse.ie

challenges.intro_fact: Yesterday was the UN International Day for Conservation of Mangrove Ecosystems. Mangroves are coastal trees that store three to five times more carbon per hectare than tropical rainforests. They protect coastlines, support fisheries, and provide nursery habitat for marine species. And they are disappearing at an alarming rate.

questions.text: Where do mangrove forests grow?
options: In tropical and subtropical coastal zones where rivers meet the sea
In sandy desert areas near the coast
questions.fact: Mangroves are found in tropical and subtropical coastal areas, particularly at river mouths and tidal zones, across Asia, Africa, the Americas, and Australia. They thrive in the transition between land and sea.

questions.text: What does 'blue carbon' mean in the context of coastal ecosystems?
options: Carbon stored in the ocean floor as fossil fuels
Carbon captured and stored in coastal and marine ecosystems such as mangroves, seagrass, and saltmarshes
Carbon emissions from shipping and maritime transport
Carbon dioxide dissolved in ocean water
questions.fact: Blue carbon refers to carbon captured and stored by coastal and marine ecosystems, including mangroves, seagrass meadows, and saltmarshes. These habitats store carbon at much higher rates per hectare than most terrestrial forests.

questions.text: Approximately how much more carbon per hectare do mangroves store compared to a typical tropical forest?
options: Three to five times as much
questions.fact: Mangrove forests store an estimated three to five times more carbon per hectare than tropical rainforests, mostly in their waterlogged soils, making their conservation a critical climate priority.

challenges.action_intro: Ireland has its own blue carbon ecosystems in saltmarshes and seagrass beds along the coast. Protecting them is Ireland's equivalent of mangrove conservation.

actions.title: Learn about Ireland's saltmarshes and seagrass beds
actions.desc: Visit npws.ie to learn about Ireland's coastal habitats. Saltmarshes are found in sheltered bays around Ireland and are some of the most carbon-dense ecosystems in the country.
actions.carbon: Builds awareness of Irish blue carbon ecosystems

actions.title: Choose only certified sustainable seafood this week
actions.desc: Sustainable fishing practices protect the coastal ecosystems -- including seagrass beds and mangrove-adjacent habitats -- that are critical for blue carbon storage. Look for the MSC label.

challenges.resources: IUCN Mangroves: iucn.org | Mangrove Action Project: mangroveactionproject.org | NPWS coastal habitats: npws.ie

challenges.intro_fact: Today is International Tiger Day. Fewer than 3,140 tigers remain free in the wild. A century ago there were around 100,000. Three tiger subspecies -- the Bali, Javan, and Caspian tiger -- have already been lost forever. The tiger's decline is not just about one charismatic animal. It is a symptom of what we are doing to nature everywhere. We are living through the sixth mass extinction.

questions.text: How many wild tigers are estimated to remain in the world today?
questions.fact: Fewer than 3,140 tigers remain free in the wild, with all surviving subspecies either endangered or critically endangered. Three subspecies have already been driven to extinction.

questions.text: The current rate of species extinction globally is estimated to be how many times higher than the natural background rate?
questions.fact: The rapid loss of species is estimated to be between 1,000 and 10,000 times higher than the natural extinction rate, with between 0.01 and 0.1% of all species becoming extinct each year.

questions.text: According to the UN, how many species are currently at risk of extinction globally?
questions.fact: The UN reports that one million species are currently at risk of extinction, while 75% of land ecosystems and two-thirds of marine environments have been significantly altered by human activity.

challenges.action_intro: Biodiversity loss is happening now, at a scale and speed that is difficult to grasp. But every action that protects habitats, reduces pollution, and changes land use makes a difference.

actions.title: Support WWF's tiger conservation work
actions.desc: Visit wwf.ie to learn about tiger conservation and how your support reaches field protection teams. Even a small monthly donation funds habitat protection and anti-poaching work.
actions.carbon: Supports habitat protection for endangered species

actions.title: Reflect on what biodiversity means to you and share it with one person
actions.desc: Biodiversity is abstract until it is personal. Think about a wild animal, plant, or landscape you love and share why it matters to you. Personal stories are the most powerful catalyst for change.

challenges.resources: WWF Tiger Conservation: wwf.org/tigers | IUCN Red List: iucnredlist.org | Biodiversity Ireland: biodiversityireland.ie

challenges.intro_fact: A cigarette butt looks small, but it takes up to 12 years to break down in nature. During that time it keeps releasing plastic fibres and toxic chemicals into the water.

questions.text: According to Clean Coasts Ireland, what share of all litter found on Irish beaches is made up of cigarette waste?
questions.fact: Research from the Department of the Environment found that cigarette waste makes up 48.4% of all litter in Ireland, and it's consistently the top item found during Clean Coasts' Big Beach Clean.

questions.text: France has started making the tobacco industry pay for cleaning up cigarette litter. What is this called?
options: The polluter pays scheme, through a body called Alcome
questions.fact: Under French law, tobacco companies now fund the collection and cleaning of cigarette litter through Alcome. Whoever makes the pollution should help pay to clean it up, rather than leaving the cost to local councils and taxpayers.

questions.text: How many cigarette butts are dropped on the ground worldwide every second?
questions.fact: Around 137,000 cigarette butts are dropped every second worldwide. A single butt can contaminate up to 500 litres of water and contains around 7,000 chemical compounds, many of them toxic.

challenges.action_intro: You do not need to smoke to help with this one. Small habits around litter make a real difference.

actions.title: Use a pocket ashtray instead of dropping the butt
actions.desc: If you smoke or vape, small tin or pouch ashtrays are cheap and stop butts washing into drains and rivers.
actions.carbon: Reduces microplastic and toxin pollution in waterways

actions.title: Pick up 3 cigarette butts next time you're out for a walk
actions.desc: It sounds small, but every butt kept out of a drain is one less source of microplastics and chemicals in the water.
actions.carbon: Prevents chemical leaching into local water systems

challenges.resources: Clean Coasts Ireland: cleancoasts.org | Surfrider Foundation Europe: surfrider.eu | EU Single-Use Plastics Directive: environment.ec.europa.eu

challenges.intro_fact: August is Green Month, a good time to build one habit that actually sticks. Ireland has the highest per capita greenhouse gas emissions in the EU, often around 50% above average. Small choices, repeated often enough, genuinely move that number.

questions.text: How does Ireland's average per capita greenhouse gas footprint compare to the rest of the EU?
questions.fact: Ireland has the highest per capita emissions in the EU, often around 50% above average, driven mostly by agriculture, transport and energy use.

questions.text: Looking at climate plans across the EU and other big emitters, which behaviour change is most commonly promoted?
options: Promoting electric vehicles and public transport
questions.fact: Encouraging electric vehicles was mentioned by 80% of countries studied, and public transport by 75%, while high-impact areas like food and flying were largely left out of climate plans.

questions.text: According to the IPCC, how much could changing our everyday habits reduce global emissions by 2050?
questions.fact: The IPCC found that the right policies and infrastructure could unlock a 40 to 70% cut in emissions through lifestyle change, calling it 'significant untapped potential' that also improves health and wellbeing.

challenges.action_intro: The trick to a habit that lasts is tying it to something you already do every day.

actions.title: Pick one new habit and attach it to something you already do
actions.desc: Like bringing a reusable cup when you get coffee, or switching off devices before bed.

actions.title: Do a 10-minute home energy check
actions.desc: Walk around your home and note anything using energy needlessly. Most fixes take minutes.
actions.carbon: Up to 100 kg CO2/year if acted on

challenges.resources: SEAI home energy tips: seai.ie | EPA Ireland emissions data: epa.ie | IPCC AR6 Summary: ipcc.ch

challenges.intro_fact: Yesterday was International Day of the World's Indigenous Peoples. Indigenous peoples make up about 5% of the global population but protect an estimated 80% of the world's remaining biodiversity. Traditional knowledge of the land is one of our oldest conservation tools, and Ireland has its own version, hidden in hedgerows.

questions.text: According to UN estimates, what share of the world's remaining biodiversity do indigenous peoples protect, despite making up only about 5% of the population?
questions.fact: Indigenous peoples protect an estimated 80% of the world's remaining biodiversity, largely through generations of traditional land management.

questions.text: Ireland has its own long tradition of land stewardship: hedgerows. How many kilometres of hedgerow does Ireland currently have?
questions.fact: Ireland has around 689,000 km of hedgerows, but numbers are declining. The Climate Action Plan targets 40,000 km of new planting to help reverse the loss.

questions.text: France has lost more than 40% of its hedgerows since the 1970s. What is its 2023 plan to reverse that called?
questions.fact: France's 2023 Hedgerow Pact aims for a net gain of 50,000 km of hedgerow by 2030, echoing the EU's push under the Common Agricultural Policy.

challenges.action_intro: You do not need farmland to help protect hedges and green corridors.

actions.title: Learn to identify 3 native hedgerow species near you
actions.desc: Blackthorn, hawthorn and hazel are common in Irish hedges.
actions.carbon: Builds awareness of local biodiversity loss

actions.title: Support a local hedgerow or tree planting scheme
actions.desc: One mature hedge can support hundreds of species.
actions.carbon: Sequesters roughly 50% more carbon than a similar area of forestry

challenges.resources: UN Indigenous Peoples Day: un.org | Ireland Climate Action Plan: gov.ie | Tree Council of Ireland: treecouncil.ie

challenges.intro_fact: Ireland feels like a rainy country, but climate change is putting real pressure on water supply, especially in summer, when demand rises just as rainfall drops.

questions.text: What is putting the greatest pressure on Dublin's water supply in the coming years?
options: Population growth combined with an ageing pipe network
questions.fact: Greater Dublin's water supply is under pressure from population growth and leaking, ageing infrastructure, which is why Uisce Éireann's Water Supply Project plans to pipe water from the River Shannon.

questions.text: Under the EU Water Framework Directive, member states must bring water bodies to 'good status'. Roughly what share of Europe's surface waters currently meet that standard?
questions.fact: Less than half of Europe's rivers, lakes and coastal waters currently meet 'good ecological status', with agricultural pollution among the main pressures.

questions.text: Global demand for fresh water is projected to grow by how much by 2050?
questions.fact: Global water demand is projected to grow by 55% by 2050, driven by population growth, agriculture and industry.

challenges.action_intro: Most water use is invisible, hidden in the food and things we buy. But a few visible habits still help.

actions.title: Fix a dripping tap this week
actions.desc: A single dripping tap can waste over 5,000 litres of water a year.
actions.carbon: Saves thousands of litres of treated water annually

actions.title: Take one minute off your shower
actions.desc: Small change, adds up fast across a household.
actions.carbon: Can save over 5,000 litres per person per year

challenges.resources: Uisce Éireann water supply project: water.ie | EPA water quality reports: epa.ie | European Environment Agency: eea.europa.eu

challenges.intro_fact: Today is both World Eagle Day and World Elephant Day. Ireland lost its white-tailed eagles over a century ago, hunted to extinction. Since 2007, a reintroduction programme has been quietly bringing them home.

questions.text: When did Ireland's white-tailed eagle reintroduction begin, bringing young birds over from Norway?
questions.fact: Ireland's reintroduction began in 2007, led by the Golden Eagle Trust, releasing young birds into Killarney National Park. The species had been extinct in Ireland since the early 1900s, largely due to persecution.

questions.text: White-tailed eagles were once nearly wiped out across most of Europe. What helped populations recover in countries like Norway, Germany and Scotland?
options: A drop in fish stocks driving eagles inland
questions.fact: Legal protection, banning harmful pesticides like DDT, and dedicated reintroduction programmes helped white-tailed eagle populations recover across Europe.

questions.text: Roughly how many African elephants are estimated to remain in the wild today, down from several million a century ago?
questions.fact: An estimated 415,000 African elephants remain in the wild, largely due to poaching for ivory and habitat loss.

challenges.action_intro: Rewilding success stories show that recovery is possible, but it needs ongoing support.

actions.title: Report white-tailed eagle sightings if you spot one
actions.desc: Golden Eagle Trust and NPWS track sightings to monitor the population.
actions.carbon: Supports population monitoring and conservation research

actions.title: Support an elephant or raptor conservation charity
actions.desc: Small, regular donations fund habitat protection and anti-poaching work.
actions.carbon: Funds habitat protection for endangered species

challenges.resources: Golden Eagle Trust: goldeneagle.ie | NPWS: npws.ie | IUCN African Elephant Status Report: iucn.org

challenges.intro_fact: Flights are one of the most carbon-heavy things most of us do, and short trips are often the worst offenders. A staycation, a low-carbon trip closer to home, can still be a proper break.

questions.text: What's one advantage Ireland has for a low-carbon holiday, compared to flying abroad?
options: Most of the country is reachable by train, bus or car
Ireland has more airports than any other country
There is no public transport in Ireland
questions.fact: Ireland's compact size means most destinations are reachable by train, bus or car, cutting out the highest-carbon part of most holidays: the flight.

questions.text: Which type of flight tends to have the highest carbon emissions per kilometre travelled?
options: Short-haul flights, because take-off and landing use a large share of the fuel
questions.fact: Short-haul flights are often the least fuel-efficient per kilometre, because take-off and landing burn a large share of total fuel regardless of distance.

questions.text: Aviation leaders admitted in 2026 that a major climate target is likely to be missed. Which one?
questions.fact: In June 2026, IATA's director general admitted aviation's net zero by 2050 pledge will 'probably not now be achieved,' citing slow sustainable fuel progress and weak policy enforcement.

challenges.action_intro: A good holiday doesn't need a flight to be memorable.

actions.title: Plan one Irish trip this year instead of flying
actions.desc: Explore a county you've never visited by train or car.
actions.carbon: Avoids the highest-carbon part of most holidays

actions.title: If you do fly, choose direct routes
actions.desc: Layovers add extra take-offs and landings, the most fuel-heavy part of a flight.
actions.carbon: Cuts unnecessary take-off and landing emissions

challenges.resources: Fáilte Ireland: failteireland.ie | IATA: iata.org | Irish Rail: irishrail.ie

challenges.intro_fact: Ireland's EPA publishes a water quality report every year. The 2025 report showed no real improvement, agricultural runoff and wastewater remain the main problems.

questions.text: According to the EPA's most recent water quality report, what are the two biggest causes of poor water quality in Ireland?
options: Excess nutrients from agriculture and wastewater
questions.fact: The EPA's annual report found no real improvement in 2025, with excess nutrients from agriculture and wastewater remaining the main problems.

questions.text: About how much of Europe's original wetlands have been lost, according to a 2026 mapping study?
questions.fact: A 2026 study from the University of Copenhagen found that about half of Europe's wetlands have been lost, and a fifth of remaining peatlands are degraded. Wetlands act as natural water filters.

questions.text: According to WHO and UNICEF, roughly how many people worldwide lack access to safely managed drinking water?
questions.fact: An estimated 2.2 billion people worldwide still lack access to safely managed drinking water, showing water quality is not just an Irish or European issue but a global one.

challenges.action_intro: Ireland's water problems come mostly from the land, not the sea, so land-based habits matter.

actions.title: Check the EPA's bathing water status before you swim
actions.desc: Takes a minute, tells you what you're getting into.
actions.carbon: Protects your own health and highlights pollution hotspots

actions.title: Cut back on garden fertiliser this month
actions.desc: Excess nutrients feed the same algae blooms affecting places like Lough Neagh.

challenges.resources: EPA bathing water quality: epa.ie | Uisce Éireann: water.ie | European Environment Agency: eea.europa.eu

challenges.intro_fact: Ireland's bogs are one of the country's biggest carbon stores, and one of its most damaged habitats. Restoring them is now a national priority.

questions.text: Peatlands cover roughly what share of Ireland's land area?
questions.fact: Peatlands cover around 1.46 million hectares, about 21% of Ireland, storing an estimated 1.6 billion tonnes of carbon.

questions.text: Roughly what share of Irish peatlands have been degraded by drainage, turf cutting, farming and forestry?
questions.fact: Up to 85% of Irish peatlands have been degraded. Only about 25% are estimated to be healthy enough to still filter water and store carbon well.

questions.text: Under the EU Nature Restoration Law, what share of drained peatlands under farming must be restored by 2030?
questions.fact: The EU Nature Restoration Law targets 30% of drained farmed peatland restored by 2030, rising to 40% by 2040 and 50% by 2050, mostly through rewetting.

challenges.action_intro: Restoring a bog mostly means rewetting it, and it's already happening at scale in Ireland.

actions.title: Learn what Bord na Móna's rehabilitation programme covers
actions.desc: It's restoring 33,000 hectares of former industrial peatland across 82 midland bogs, over half already done.
actions.carbon: Supports Ireland's largest peatland carbon restoration programme

actions.title: Visit a restored bog walk near you
actions.desc: Many restored midland bogs now have boardwalks and trails, a good way to see peatland recovery firsthand.
actions.carbon: Builds public support for peatland restoration

challenges.resources: Bord na Móna: bordnamona.ie | Irish Peatland Conservation Council: ipcc.ie | EU Nature Restoration Law: environment.ec.europa.eu

challenges.intro_fact: Back to school season means a fresh wave of uniforms, stationery and bags, and a fresh wave of waste if we're not careful.

questions.text: Green-Schools, run by An Taisce, is one of the largest environmental education programmes in the world. Roughly how many schools in Ireland are registered?
questions.fact: Over 4,000 schools across Ireland are registered with the Green-Schools programme, covering nearly every primary and secondary school in the country.

questions.text: On average, how much water does it take to make a single pair of jeans, like the ones some school uniforms use?
questions.fact: A single pair of jeans has an average footprint of around 7,000 litres of water, the equivalent of 285 showers, and about 25kg of CO2.

questions.text: The EU's Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation, which will eventually cover textiles, aims to do what?
options: Set new EU-wide rules on durability, repairability and recyclability of products
questions.fact: The EU's Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation sets new rules on how durable, repairable and recyclable products, eventually including textiles, must be designed to be.

challenges.action_intro: Small swaps at the start of the school year add up across a whole class, or a whole school.

actions.title: Check for a uniform swap or secondhand scheme at school
actions.desc: Many parent associations run informal swaps, worth asking before buying new.
actions.carbon: Extends the useful life of school uniforms

actions.title: Reuse stationery and bags from last year where you can
actions.desc: A working schoolbag or pencil case doesn't need replacing just because it's a new year.
actions.carbon: Reduces demand for new school supplies

challenges.resources: An Taisce Green-Schools: greenschoolsireland.org | EU Ecodesign Regulation: environment.ec.europa.eu | Rediscovery Centre: rediscoverycentre.ie

challenges.intro_fact: Ireland's energy system is being rebuilt around wind, and the targets are ambitious.

questions.text: Ireland's Climate Action Plan targets what share of electricity to come from renewable sources by 2030?
questions.fact: Ireland's target is 80% of electricity from renewable sources by 2030, up from current levels, with wind expected to supply the majority of that.

questions.text: Two floating offshore wind projects planned off Cork and Clare could add how much combined capacity?
questions.fact: The Emerald and Western Star floating wind projects off Cork and Clare could add a combined 2.65 GW of offshore wind capacity, part of a wider plan to scale up Ireland's offshore wind industry.

questions.text: As countries electrify transport and heating to cut emissions, what generally happens to electricity demand?
questions.fact: Ireland's own electricity demand is projected to grow 3 to 4 times by 2050 as transport, heating and industry increasingly run on electricity instead of fossil fuels.

challenges.action_intro: A cleaner grid is coming, but a few habits help make the most of it right now.

actions.title: Check what share of your electricity supplier's mix is renewable
actions.desc: Most Irish suppliers publish a fuel mix disclosure, worth a look.

actions.title: Time energy-heavy tasks for windier days if you can
actions.desc: Ireland's grid runs cleanest when wind output is high, small timing shifts help.
actions.carbon: Shifts demand toward cleaner grid periods

challenges.resources: SEAI: seai.ie | Wind Energy Ireland: windenergyireland.com | EirGrid: eirgrid.ie

challenges.intro_fact: Barbecue and garden season brings its own wave of food and green waste, most of which doesn't need to go in the general bin at all.

questions.text: South Korea has one of the highest food waste recycling rates in the world. Roughly what share of its food waste is composted or recycled, rather than landfilled?
questions.fact: South Korea sends close to 100% of its food waste to composting or recycling, through mandatory nationwide food waste collection, among the highest rates in the world.

questions.text: What goes in Ireland's brown bin, alongside food waste?
options: Light garden waste and compostable packaging
questions.fact: Ireland's brown bin takes cooked and raw food, light garden waste and compostable packaging, all of which go for anaerobic digestion or composting rather than landfill.

questions.text: Composting food waste instead of landfilling it cuts its climate impact by roughly how much?
questions.fact: Composting food and garden waste instead of sending it to landfill cuts its climate impact by more than 90%, mainly by avoiding methane from anaerobic decomposition in landfill.

challenges.action_intro: A little planning goes a long way in barbecue season.

actions.title: Use your brown bin for garden and food waste this BBQ season
actions.desc: Grass clippings and food scraps belong there, not the general bin.
actions.carbon: Diverts waste from landfill to composting

actions.title: Portion your BBQ food a little more carefully
actions.desc: Overcatering is one of the most common causes of summer food waste. A rough headcount plan helps.
actions.carbon: Reduces food waste at the source

challenges.intro_fact: As the evenings draw in, Ireland's bats are out in force, feeding up before the colder months. They're the country's only mammals capable of true flight.

questions.text: How many resident bat species does Ireland have, all of them legally protected?
questions.fact: Ireland has 9 resident bat species, all protected under Irish and EU law. Bats are the only Irish mammals capable of true flight.

questions.text: Ireland's rarest bat, the lesser horseshoe bat, is found mainly in which part of the country?
options: The western counties (Clare, Cork, Galway, Kerry, Limerick, Mayo)
questions.fact: The lesser horseshoe bat, Ireland's rarest bat species, is found almost entirely in the western counties, particularly Clare, Cork, Galway, Kerry, Limerick and Mayo.

questions.text: A single small bat, like a common pipistrelle, can eat roughly how many insects in one night?
questions.fact: A common pipistrelle bat can eat up to around 3,000 insects in a single night, making bats one of nature's most effective pest controllers.

challenges.action_intro: Bats need very little from us, mostly just a bit of dark, undisturbed space.

actions.title: Join a bat walk this month
actions.desc: Many local heritage or biodiversity groups run evening bat walks with bat detectors.
actions.carbon: Builds appreciation and awareness of local biodiversity

actions.title: Leave a corner of your garden a little wild
actions.desc: Long grass and native shrubs attract the insects bats feed on.
actions.carbon: Supports local insect and bat populations

challenges.intro_fact: Late summer is a critical window for Ireland's pollinators, stocking up on the last flowers before winter. Ivy and heather matter more than people think.

questions.text: According to the All-Ireland Pollinator Plan, roughly what share of Ireland's wild bee species are at risk of extinction?
questions.fact: About one-third of Ireland's wild bee species are threatened with extinction, mainly due to loss of food sources and nesting sites.

questions.text: The All-Ireland Pollinator Plan's advice on mowing is often surprising. What does it actually recommend?
options: Mow as often as possible for a tidy lawn
Mow less often, and let common wildflowers grow naturally
Only use generic wildflower seed mixes
questions.fact: The plan's 'Don't Mow, Let It Grow' approach recommends reducing mowing frequency to let common wildflowers grow naturally, rather than relying on generic wildflower seed mixes, which can sometimes do more harm than good.

questions.text: Roughly what share of the food we eat depends on pollinators like bees?
questions.fact: Bees and other pollinators are responsible for pollinating roughly a third of everything we eat, from apples to almonds.

challenges.action_intro: Small, low-effort changes in late summer make a real difference to pollinators heading into autumn.

actions.title: Let one patch of your garden or green space grow wild this month
actions.desc: Late summer wildflowers like ivy and heather are a vital late-season food source for bees.
actions.carbon: Supports pollinator food sources before winter

actions.title: Check if your workplace or community group is on the AIPP list
actions.desc: Businesses, schools and community groups can sign up to take specific pollinator-friendly actions.

challenges.intro_fact: Ireland has a strong charity shop culture, a genuine head start on textile reuse most countries don't have.

questions.text: On average, how much water does it take to make a single pair of jeans?
questions.fact: A single pair of jeans has an average footprint of around 7,000 litres of water, the equivalent of 285 showers, and about 25kg of CO2.

questions.text: What is Ireland's national centre dedicated to promoting the circular economy, based in Ballymun, Dublin?
questions.fact: The Rediscovery Centre in Ballymun is Ireland's national centre for the circular economy, running reuse and upcycling programmes including a dedicated furniture and textiles reuse workshop.

questions.text: French jeans maker 1083 designed a jean intended to be recycled indefinitely, backed by what kind of system?
questions.fact: French jeans maker 1083 manufactures entirely in France to cut transport emissions and designed a jean intended to be recycled indefinitely, backed by a refundable deposit system.

challenges.action_intro: Ireland has a strong charity shop culture, worth using before buying new.

actions.title: Try repairing one item before replacing it
actions.desc: A patch, a stitch or a cobbler visit often costs far less than buying new.
actions.carbon: Extends the useful life of existing garments

actions.title: Drop unwanted textiles at a proper collection point, not the general bin
actions.desc: Textile banks and charity shops keep clothing in reuse rather than landfill.
actions.carbon: Diverts textiles from landfill into reuse

challenges.intro_fact: Coastal erosion is no longer a distant risk for Ireland, it's already reshaping parts of the Dublin coastline and beyond.

questions.text: How fast is sea level rising in Dublin Bay, compared to the global average?
options: About the same as the global average
Roughly double the global average, at 7-8mm a year
questions.fact: Water levels in Dublin Bay are rising at 7-8mm a year, roughly double the global average of 3-4mm a year.

questions.text: At Portrane Beach in north Dublin, what scheme has been introduced to help homeowners move away from eroding coastline?
questions.fact: A Voluntary Homeowners Relocation Scheme has been introduced at Portrane, an example of 'planned retreat,' moving people away from land that's no longer safe to build on.

questions.text: What is the current global average rate of sea level rise, the baseline Dublin Bay is rising about twice as fast as?
questions.fact: Global sea levels are rising by roughly 3-4mm a year on average, making Dublin Bay's 7-8mm a year roughly double the global rate.

challenges.action_intro: Coastal change is already happening, knowing your own area's risk is a good first step.

actions.title: Learn if your area has a local coastal or flood risk plan
actions.desc: Local authority websites often have flood risk maps, worth checking if you're near the coast or a river.
actions.carbon: Builds awareness of local climate risk

actions.title: Support dune and coastal habitat restoration where you can
actions.desc: Healthy dune systems act as a natural buffer against erosion and storm surges.

challenges.intro_fact: Europe holds an uncomfortable record: it's the fastest-warming continent on the planet, and 2025 showed exactly what that means in practice.

questions.text: Europe is warming faster than the global average. Roughly how much faster, according to recent analysis?
questions.fact: Europe is the world's fastest-warming continent, warming roughly twice as fast as the global average since 1980.

questions.text: In 2025, European wildfires released a record amount of carbon. Roughly how much?
questions.fact: European wildfires emitted 47 million tonnes of carbon in 2025, a record, with Spain, the UK, the Netherlands, Germany and Cyprus all breaking previous fire-emission records.

questions.text: How much more likely did climate change make the extreme hot, dry, windy conditions behind Portugal and Spain's 2025 wildfires?
questions.fact: Climate change made the extreme conditions behind Portugal and Spain's 2025 wildfires at least 40 times more likely, according to attribution research.

challenges.action_intro: Heatwaves are becoming a genuine Irish concern too, not just a southern European one.

actions.title: Check in on elderly or vulnerable neighbours during a heatwave
actions.desc: Heat-related illness is a real and growing risk, even in Ireland's traditionally mild summers.

actions.title: Learn your area's wildfire risk if you're near forest or gorse land
actions.desc: Ireland has seen its own gorse and forest fires in dry spells, knowing the risk helps you act early.

challenges.resources: New Scientist, April 2026 | Met Éireann: met.ie | Copernicus Climate Change Service: climate.copernicus.eu

challenges.intro_fact: Dublin hosts an academic conference on ecosystems and biodiversity this week, part of a growing effort to connect nature science with real-world decisions, including business ones.

questions.text: According to WWF's Living Planet Report, monitored wildlife populations have declined by roughly how much since 1970?
questions.fact: WWF's Living Planet Report found an average 73% decline in monitored wildlife populations since 1970, one of the starkest measures of the scale of biodiversity loss.

questions.text: Ireland's most recent official assessment of protected habitats under the EU Habitats Directive found what?
options: Nearly all habitats are in good condition
The majority of assessed habitats are in unfavourable condition
questions.fact: Ireland's most recent Article 17 report found the large majority of assessed habitats in unfavourable conservation status, underlining why events like Dublin's Ecosystems and Biodiversity Conference matter.

questions.text: What is the name of the international framework helping companies disclose their impact on nature?
questions.fact: TNFD, the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures, is an international framework helping companies assess and disclose their dependencies and impacts on nature, growing fast since its 2023 launch.

challenges.action_intro: Science only matters if it reaches the people making decisions, including all of us.

actions.title: Follow research updates from Irish biodiversity conferences
actions.desc: Universities and NPWS often share key findings publicly after events like this.

actions.title: Share one surprising biodiversity fact with someone this week
actions.desc: Awareness is often the first step toward support for conservation funding and policy.
actions.carbon: Builds broader public support for conservation

challenges.resources: NPWS: npws.ie | TNFD: tnfd.global | WWF Living Planet Report: wwf.org

challenges.intro_fact: September brings both Organic September and Second-Hand September. Before we get there, it's worth knowing just how big fashion's environmental footprint actually is.

questions.text: Roughly what share of global carbon emissions does the fashion industry produce?
questions.fact: The fashion industry accounts for around 10% of global emissions, more than international flights and shipping combined, and is the second-largest consumer of water worldwide.

questions.text: What happens to most of the materials used in fashion production?
options: Most are recycled into new clothes
Roughly 87% ends up incinerated or in landfill
questions.fact: An estimated 87% of materials used in fashion end up incinerated or in landfill, despite how reusable much of it could be.

questions.text: From July 2026, what did the EU ban large companies from doing to unsold clothing?
questions.fact: From July 2026, the EU bans large companies from destroying unsold clothing, aiming to stop the practice of shredding or binning perfectly good garments that didn't sell.

challenges.action_intro: You don't need to buy anything new to take part in September's challenges, that's kind of the point.

actions.title: Do a wardrobe audit this weekend
actions.desc: Count how many items you haven't worn in a year, a good sign of what you could sell, swap or donate.
actions.carbon: Highlights overconsumption without needing a purchase

actions.title: Look up your nearest clothes swap or charity shop
actions.desc: Ireland has a strong charity shop culture, check what's already out there before buying new.
actions.carbon: Extends the useful life of existing garments

challenges.resources: EU unsold clothing ban: environment.ec.europa.eu | Rediscovery Centre Ireland: rediscoverycentre.ie | The Rewearable circular fashion guide

challenges.intro_fact: Second-Hand September challenges you to buy only pre-loved items for a month. Ireland already has a head start, with a long tradition of charity shops.

questions.text: About how many charity shops does Ireland have, according to Charity Retail Ireland?
questions.fact: Ireland has over 700 charity shops nationwide, giving the country a strong head start for a month of buying only second-hand.

questions.text: Second-Hand September started as a UK campaign. What's the idea behind it?
options: Buy only secondhand clothes for the month
Give away one item a day
questions.fact: Second-Hand September, started by Oxfam, challenges people to buy only pre-loved items, no new purchases, for the whole month.

questions.text: Since January 2025, EU law requires member states to do what with used textiles?
options: Collect them separately, rather than throwing them in general waste
questions.fact: Since January 2025, EU law requires member states to collect used textiles separately, rather than letting them go into general household waste, to boost reuse and recycling.

challenges.action_intro: One month, no new clothes purchases. See how far your wardrobe actually stretches.

actions.title: Take the Second-Hand September pledge
actions.desc: Commit to buying nothing new this month. Try a charity shop, swap, or online secondhand marketplace first.
actions.carbon: Avoids emissions from new garment production

actions.title: Sell or donate 5 items you no longer wear
actions.desc: Someone else's secondhand find starts with your own wardrobe.
actions.carbon: Extends the useful life of existing garments
